data.description:
Golden Weekly is a weekly blockchain industry summary column launched by Golden Finance, covering key news, mining information, project updates, technological advancements, and other industry dynamics.

    Headlines

    ▌Behind the Record-Breaking IPOs of Anthropic and SpaceX: Underwriters Complain About Complex Transaction Processes

    On November 22, SpaceX and Anthropic completed record-breaking IPOs this year, with underwriters receiving over $500 million in fees each. However, some bankers involved in the transactions privately complained about the complex process and stringent restrictions, which were drastically different from previous IPOs. According to sources, SpaceX's listing process was entirely led by Musk's team, strictly controlling information disclosure, stock recommendations, and allocation size. Some banks even signed contracts without knowing their underwriting fees.

    Anthropic required some underwriting banks to limit their trading teams to four senior bankers and to sign non-compete agreements with some bank executives, prohibiting core trading team members from providing services to competitors such as OpenAI, Cursor, DeepSeek, and HuggingFace within six months of the company's IPO. Additionally, the company shared documents through the NetRoadshow platform and tracked bankers' access records to prevent information leaks, but this also increased the workload for the underwriting team. On November 22, the cross-chain exchange protocol Chainflip confirmed that attackers stole approximately $12 million worth of Bitcoin, Ethereum, and stablecoins from its vault on November 21, up from the initially reported $4.86 million. Specifically, the stolen assets amounted to 122.86 BTC, 520.22 ETH, 3.25 million USDC, and 758,141 USDT. Chainflip Labs offered the attackers a 10% bounty if they returned the remaining 90% of the stolen assets by 18:38 UTC on November 23 (2:38 Beijing time on November 24), and promised to treat the case as white-hat hacking and withdraw their complaint against law enforcement. The company stated that it had traced the attack preparations back to the validator account funded by Tornado Cash on November 11 and registered last Friday, and had obtained the attackers' identity information. According to CoinGecko data, FLIP tokens fell 42.9% in the past 24 hours. On November 22, Justin Sun, founder of TRON, posted on the X platform: "I am interested in purchasing existing shares of ByteDance, less than 5%. Those interested can contact me." Previously, investor Duan Yongping stated on Xueqiu that several people had recently privately tried to sell him shares. He only invests in listed companies because it's simpler and less troublesome, requiring no private dealings with anyone.

    ▌Duan Yongping: Several People Have Recently Privately Approached Him to Sell ByteDance Shares; Investing Only in Listed Companies is Simple and Convenient

    On November 22, investor Duan Yongping (Snowball ID "大道无形我有型") stated in a reply to a user on Snowball on November 21 that several people have recently privately tried to contact him to sell their ByteDance shares, which is why he came forward to explain. Duan Yongping stated: "A very important reason why I only invest in listed companies is that it's simple and convenient; I don't need to deal with anyone privately."

    ▌Four Tech Giants' Capital Expenditures Exceed Operating Cash Flow by $50.5 Billion

    Data from Coin Bureau shows that the combined capital expenditures of the four tech giants—Amazon, Alphabet, Oracle, and Meta—exceeded their operating cash flow by approximately $50.5 billion.

    Among them, Amazon exceeded its capital expenditure by approximately $34.8 billion, Alphabet by approximately $9.1 billion, Oracle by approximately $5.4 billion, and Meta by approximately $1.2 billion. Of the five major US cloud computing companies surveyed, only Microsoft's operating cash flow was sufficient to cover its capital expenditures. Microsoft's operating cash flow was approximately $58 billion, capital expenditures were approximately $39.4 billion, leaving a balance of approximately $18.6 billion.

    Policy

    ▌Shanghai and Shenzhen Stock Exchanges Lower Margin Ratio Minimum to 80%, Theoretically Could Bring Nearly 400 Billion Yuan in Incremental Funds

    On November 22, with the approval of the China Securities Regulatory Commission, the Shanghai and Shenzhen Stock Exchanges lowered the margin ratio minimum from 100% to 80%, effective November 30, 2026.

    It is estimated that this adjustment could theoretically bring in nearly 400 billion yuan in incremental funds. The South Korean government is preparing to launch a stock market stabilization fund, relax buyback restrictions, and crack down on illegal short selling. On November 22, the South Korean Ministry of Finance and Economy announced that a joint emergency market situation review meeting, chaired by Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance and Economy Lee Hyung-il, was held that day at the government office building in Seoul. The meeting decided to implement the following market stabilization measures. First, the government will work to improve the activation mechanism of the stock market stabilization fund and enhance its operational effectiveness to ensure it can be activated at any time according to market conditions. Second, starting November 24, the government will relax the daily upper limit on the number of treasury stock purchase orders submitted by listed companies for the next three months. This move aims to encourage companies to expand stock buybacks, thereby alleviating downward pressure on the stock market. The government will also strengthen monitoring of illegal short selling. The Financial Supervisory Service of Korea and the Korea Exchange will conduct a three-month special monitoring campaign, and any illegal activities discovered will be dealt with seriously. In addition, the government will closely monitor credit financing transactions, unsettled transactions, and forced liquidations to prevent further escalation of chain-reaction selling pressure and exacerbation of market volatility. On November 22, Michael Handelsman, an attorney at Kelman Law, wrote that Section 4(a)(11) of the GENIUS Act, which restricts issuers from paying interest on stablecoins, will take effect on January 18, 2027. This date was confirmed by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency's final rule on October 23. At that time, regulated stablecoin issuers will be prohibited from paying interest or income solely for the holder's holding, use, or retention of stablecoins, in the form of cash, tokens, or other consideration. The article states that rewards funded by the exchange itself and not compensated by the issuer are not subject to this restriction; if the issuer pays an equivalent amount to the exchange and designates the distribution, regulators have substantial grounds to determine that the exchange is paying interest on behalf of the issuer. This restriction applies equally to retail and institutional holders, with no minimum amount exemption. The article also points out that arrangements requiring users to lend tokens to receive rewards require separate securities law analysis, citing the SEC's 2022 BlockFi case for comparison. On November 21, the Government of the People's Republic of China and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) signed the "Agreement between the Government of the People's Republic of China and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank on the Establishment of an Office in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China" in Hong Kong, laying the foundation for the AIIB to open an office in Hong Kong. The agreement was signed by the Minister of Finance of the People's Republic of China, Lan Fu'an, and the President of the AIIB, Zou Jiayi. The agreement establishes the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) office in Hong Kong and sets out principles for privileges, waivers, and other matters conducive to its establishment. Hong Kong Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po stated that the AIIB's choice to establish an office in Hong Kong fully affirms Hong Kong's status as an international financial center and highlights its unique role in attracting international capital and supporting Asian infrastructure development. The Hong Kong SAR Government will fully support the establishment and operation of the office and looks forward to strengthening cooperation with the AIIB to leverage Hong Kong's capital markets and professional services to provide greater support for its business development and attract more international capital to participate in Asian infrastructure investment and financing. On the same day, Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Chan Ho-lim, on behalf of the Hong Kong SAR Government, signed an agreement with AIIB Chief Partnership Officer Kim Heon to inject US$20 million into the "Special Fund for Project Preparation" to demonstrate support for the AIIB's work.

    ▌US Representatives Introduce Bill to Establish Whistleblower Mechanism for Prediction Market Insider Trading

    On November 21, US Representatives Sean Casten and Ted Lieu introduced the "Prediction Market Insider Trading Regulatory Act," which proposes establishing a whistleblower mechanism within the US Department of Justice, allowing whistleblowers to anonymously provide information on prediction market fraud. According to the bill, whistleblowers may receive a reward if their information leads to successful enforcement action. Casten stated that this measure aims to encourage reporting of misconduct and combat insider trading in prediction markets.

    Blockchain and AI Applications ▌Claude's Contribution to a Proof of the Riemann Hypothesis Published, Awaiting Independent Verification On November 20th, according to an unsigned statement published on the personal website of Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge, the author claims to believe that he and Claude have found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, and that the same method can also solve the generalized Riemann Hypothesis. The statement includes 14 volumes of Lean formal proof code; the related arguments still await independent verification.

    ▌Lagarde: Tokenization Could Facilitate a Single European Digital Asset Market

    On November 20, European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde stated at the European Banking Conference in Frankfurt that, within a proper framework, tokenization offers an opportunity to establish a unified European digital asset single market from the outset. She noted that the ECB is collaborating with market participants through the Appia project to promote an integrated market, including common standards; in addition to infrastructure, legislators also need to develop common rules. She mentioned that the global tokenized asset market reached approximately €23 billion in March of this year, five times the size of a year ago.

    ...

    ▌Research: Bitcoin Wallet Signature Random Number Reuse Can Be Exploited by Bots in Seconds

    On November 20th, researchers Vincent Jacquot and Benoît Donnet from the University of Liège published an experiment showing that when a Bitcoin wallet's private key is leaked due to the reuse of signature random numbers, an automated program can launch an attack within one to several seconds. In the experiment, at least two competing transactions attempted to obtain bait funds. The researchers scanned relevant signatures on six blockchains from their launch to June 30, 2024, recovering a total of 3,620 private keys, of which 3,278 came from the Bitcoin network. Based on prices as of November 25, 2024, the combined historical peak balance of the relevant addresses was approximately $106 million; this figure assumes that each address was attacked at its peak balance, and the study did not determine the actual amount stolen.

    OpenAI Report: Internal Agents' API Equivalent Value is Twice That of Researchers' Non-Equity Compensation OpenAI released an internal research report, "Research Acceleration: The Jagged Frontier." The report states that in October, the median daily API cost per agent call per researcher was $2,400, a 62% increase from September; the 90th percentile was $23,000, a 105% increase. Based on an 8-hour "Agent workday," each researcher drives an average of 5.7 agents per day, 11 times the previous benchmark; over two-thirds of researchers run at least 4 agents simultaneously during peak periods, and over 10% run more than 16 simultaneously. In September, the API equivalent value of an agent was approximately twice that of a researcher's non-equity compensation, but internal agent usage accounted for only 2% of total research computing power. The agent can independently complete 46% of research tasks that previously required 2-4 hours, compared to 23% in March; the monitoring training success rate is 79%, and the writing of inference and service code is only 25%. On November 20th, Musk posted on X that Tesla's AI, running on its self-developed in-vehicle computer AI4, can now reach Torment II difficulty in Diablo. The post did not specify the model used, the game version, or whether manual operation was required, nor did it include videos or third-party verification; as of press time, Tesla has not released any technical documentation. Torment is the name used for high difficulty levels in Diablo III and Diablo IV, with Torment II being a lower level; AI4 is Tesla's self-developed in-vehicle inference computer used for Full Self-Driving (FSD). Cryptocurrency ▌A whale deposited 2,279 BTC, worth approximately $134.7 million, into Binance. According to Lookonchain monitoring on November 22, an address, bc1qa2cv0p92t727kd9q6f87vqra72zf3cytdgeqyh, deposited 2,279 BTC, worth approximately $134.7 million, into Binance about two hours prior.

    ▌Former Mt. Gox CEO Questions Pump.fun's Discontinuation of Wallet Login and Requirement for Users to Paste Private Keys

    On November 22, former Mt. Gox CEO Mark Karpelès published an article questioning Pump.fun's login method change, criticizing the platform for discontinuing wallet login while suggesting users paste their private keys to the website, and mentioning the risks of wallet leaks and phishing attacks. According to Pump.fun, starting at 11 PM Beijing time on November 30, the web version will stop using external wallet login, replacing it with email or Google, Apple, or GitHub accounts; one migration method to retain existing accounts involves entering the wallet's private key, and users can also create new accounts and transfer funds. Pump.fun claims that the entered private key will be encrypted in the browser and stored by the login service provider Privy in an end-to-end encrypted manner.

    The total market capitalization of stablecoins has fallen to $284.215 billion, a new low for the year. This represents a decrease of $30.177 billion from the year's high of $314.392 billion on May 17th, a drop of approximately 9.60%. The total market capitalization of stablecoins has decreased by 1.61% and 6.15% over the past 7 and 30 days, respectively. Since entering the fourth quarter, the total market capitalization of stablecoins has continued to decline, falling to $298.741 billion at the end of October and further to $288.02 billion on November 18th. Hyperliquid's revenue reached $21.22 million in the past 7 days, ranking third on the protocol revenue list. Hyperliquid's revenue in the past 24 hours reached $3.22 million, ranking third on the protocol revenue list, behind only Tether ($17.02 million) and Circle ($6.74 million). In the past 7 days, Hyperliquid's revenue reached $21.22 million, a 15.51% increase compared to the previous 7 days. Bitcoin prices once fell by more than 16%, dipping to $55,130, before rebounding above $60,000. During the same period, Hyperliquid's perpetual contract trading volume reached $81.835 billion, a 14.35% increase compared to the previous 7 days, with a liquidation scale of approximately $1.289 billion. The perpetual contracts segment contributed $20.57 million in revenue, accounting for approximately 97% of total revenue. (DefiLlama)

    ▌CryptoQuant Analyst: Binance BTC Funding Fees Turn Negative, Bearish Sentiment in Derivatives Market

    On November 22, CryptoQuant analyst Darkfost wrote that Binance's Bitcoin funding fees have turned negative, and bearish sentiment in the derivatives market is intensifying. He pointed out that at the time of writing, Bitcoin had fallen 56.3% from its all-time high and 17.4% since November; historically, concentrated bearish sentiment often appears after a significant correction and may become a noteworthy contrarian signal. However, Darkfost emphasized that a negative funding fee is not a reliable reversal signal, and historically, there have been instances where a negative funding fee only led to a brief rebound.

    **Important Economic Developments** ▌Fuel Costs Have Squeezed US Flights, and the Risk of Shutdown Lies at Year-End On November 22, the current temporary funding for the United States expires on December 11. According to CNN, Trump, citing reasons such as dealing with the Iran war, has demanded hundreds of billions of dollars more in addition to the existing defense budget, but the source of funding and spending priorities remain controversial. Leaders of both parties favor passing another temporary funding, but both sides expect negotiations to be largely stalled before the Senate Democratic leadership election on December 1. If a formal budget or extension of temporary funding is not passed by December 11, the federal government will shut down on December 12. High fuel costs this year have led airlines to cut low-profit routes. Last year, from the Saturday before Christmas to the first Sunday of the new year, the Transportation Security Administration screened an average of about 140,000 more people per day than usual, and major airlines still have strong bookings this year. Aviation industry analyst Zach Griff pointed out that if the shutdown leads to staff shortages in security and air traffic control, coupled with tight scheduling and winter snow, delays and cancellations will be even more difficult to handle. Flight disruptions still depend on whether funding can be continued and the personnel and weather conditions at that time.

    ▌Iran claims to have hit an F-16 fighter jet

    On November 21, according to Iranian media reports, Iranian air defense systems intercepted and hit an F-16 fighter jet over the Persian Gulf on November 20. The aircraft was damaged and made an emergency landing at an airport.

    ▌French Presidential Palace says latest EU budget proposal "very disappointing"

    On November 21, the French presidential palace stated on Saturday that the latest negotiating proposal for the next round of long-term budget negotiations for the EU was "deeply disappointing."

    The French presidential palace stated in a statement: "The plan falls far short of what is needed, especially in terms of the Common Agricultural Policy, particularly in its inability to guarantee income support for farmers. As it stands, the plan proposed by the President of the European Council cannot serve as the basis for an agreement." On November 21st, according to CCTV, on the 20th local time, US President Trump again criticized the Federal Reserve, saying that current interest rates are too high and that the Fed's decisions have a "political nature." However, he said that his statement was not directed at Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh. Analysts believe that Warsh, nominated by Trump, is now facing a practical dilemma. On the one hand, Trump wants to lower interest rates to boost the market and alleviate debt repayment pressure; on the other hand, persistently high inflation makes the Fed hesitant to cut rates. Warsh needs to find a balance between the political demands of the White House and the independence of the central bank's monetary policy.

    ▌BNK Report: Storage Demand Has Peaked, SK Hynix's Current Stock Price Is Not Undervalued

    On November 21st, Citrini analyst Jukan published an article on the X platform stating that a research report on SK Hynix released a few days prior by BNK Investment & Securities argued that storage demand has peaked, and SK Hynix is ​​not undervalued even at its current stock price. This institution became the first South Korean sell-side firm to downgrade SK Hynix's rating from "buy" to "hold" in late April of this year, effectively issuing a sell recommendation for the storage industry.

data.title: Why is it difficult for revenue repatriation to drive up cryptocurrency prices? Net repatriation has only a weak correlation with price.

Author: @heytranks; Translator: AididiaoJP, Foresight News

More and more protocols are returning revenue to token holders, with buybacks, burns, and fee distribution becoming new focal points. Hyperliquid uses most of its revenue to buy back native tokens, prompting more projects to follow suit. But can these mechanisms really drive up token prices?

According to DefiLlama data, among 83 major tokens with annual revenue of at least $10 million or at least $1 million in token holder return, 66 have established return mechanisms. 76% of these were launched in 2025 or later. These mechanisms can be broadly categorized into three types: burn, holding, and distribution.

Three Ways to Return Value

Over the past 12 months, the protocol has returned approximately $2.12 billion. Of this, $1.4 billion was burned, accounting for 66%; and of this $1.4 billion, 76% came from Hyperliquid ($602 million), Tron ($333 million), and Pump.fun ($133 million). The large amount burned is not due to higher burning efficiency, but because the highest-revenue protocols chose to burn.

data.title: The fastest way to stop the Fed from raising interest rates: US stocks threatening to collapse.
data.description:
Author: Pan Lingfei, Wall Street Insights

Bank of America's chief investment strategist, Michael Hartnett, pointed out in his latest Flow Show this week that the fastest way to stop the Federal Reserve from continuing to raise interest rates is to make the stock market give back all of its gains in 2026. This target corresponds to 6,845 points for the S&P 500, which closed at 6,925 points last Friday, leaving only 80 points, or about 1.2%, to reach the trigger point. After maintaining a "risk-averse" stance for six consecutive weeks, Hartnett's framework is turning from prediction into market reality.

Last week, US stocks recorded their worst weekly performance since "Liberation Day".

The S&P 500 fell 8.4% for the week, marking its seventh consecutive day of decline and breaking below the 200-day moving average, entering a technical correction. The Nasdaq 100 has fallen 19.8% from its October record high, nearing the edge of a bear market. The VIX briefly broke through 39. According to Hartnett, the S&P 500's year-to-date gain has narrowed to 1.2% from 10.9% a week ago. The market has begun to "work" for the Federal Reserve. During trading last Friday, Fed Governor Waller's proposed 50-basis-point "shocking" rate hike was removed from the options, the probability of a January rate hike fell below 60%, and the 10-year Treasury yield fell below 5%. However, statements from Fed officials did not soften: Governor Cook stated that financial conditions remained too loose, Philadelphia Fed's Paulson was open to consecutive rate hikes, and the meeting minutes showed that almost all officials believed further tightening was necessary. Hartnett's assessment is that if the Federal Reserve remains a "good friend" of Wall Street, then widening credit spreads and a stock market decline will prematurely end the rate hike cycle, triggered by the S&P 500 falling below 6,845 points and the IG CDX rising above 80 basis points. However, if the Fed becomes a true inflation fighter after the midterm elections, the risk of a hard landing will increase, and the market will not price in a "peak interest rate" until the earliest interest rate meeting on March 18th or April 28th next year. "The Fastest Way to Stop the Fed": Two Numbers and Two Thresholds" Hartnett summarizes the logic of this round in one sentence: "The fastest way to stop the Fed is for the stock market to give back all of its gains this year." The S&P 500 is projected to close at 6,845 points in 2025, which he considers the first threshold for judging a policy shift. The other threshold is in the credit market. Investment-grade CDX broke through 80 basis points last week, and the cash-investment-grade spread widened by about 10 basis points in a single week, the widest since May 2025. The pressure on both the stock and bond markets constitutes what he calls the transmission chain of "the market doing the Fed's bidding." Goldman Sachs gives the same assessment of the mechanism. According to Goldman Sachs, a stock market decline is the only factor that can prevent interest rate hikes; Goldman Sachs' Tony Pasquariello, however, asked last Friday whether the Fed is about to "get serious." The disagreement lies in the magnitude of the move. Hartnett believes 6,845 points is enough to force the Fed to back down; however, critics point out that a Fed that has failed to meet its inflation target for 67 consecutive months, has three overheated CPI reports on its desk, and has just witnessed voters punishing the ruling party for inflation, needs far more than a zero-growth S&P 500 for the year. The experience of 2018 was a 20% drop, and at that time the Fed did not have an inflation problem. The dollar outperformed the S&P 500, while gold and Bitcoin became "positions". Hartnett's annual performance rankings show a clear contraction in risk assets: crude oil rose 44.9%, the dollar rose 5.7%, US stocks rose 4.8%, global stocks rose 4.4%, and cash rose 3.3%; high-yield bonds fell 1.2%, investment-grade bonds fell 3.0%, government bonds fell 3.9%, gold fell 15.1%, and Bitcoin fell 29.5%. Within a week, the year-to-date gain for US stocks fell from 10.9% to 4.8% (as of last Thursday), and the Nasdaq turned negative for the year. The lead of crude oil narrowed for the third consecutive week, from 54.0% to 44.9%; the two major "currency devaluation hedge" assets went from "bad" to "bad": gold widened from -10.4% to -15.1%, and Bitcoin widened from -18.9% to -29.5%. The only gainer was the US dollar, rising from 4.9% to 5.7%, meaning the dollar will outperform the S&P 500 by 2026, rendering the "buy everything except the dollar" trade ineffective.

As of last Friday's close, the situation further deteriorated: the S&P 500 rose only 1.2% year-to-date, gold fell to $3,500, and Bitcoin dropped below $60,000, hitting a new low since September 2024. As previously indicated by The Market Earn, the deleveraging of gold is far from over.

Hartnett used a chart comparing the dollar and the turning points of Federal Reserve policy to explain why he cares about "which Fed" will emerge.

Hartnett used a chart comparing the dollar and the turning points of Federal Reserve policy to explain why he cares about "which Fed" will emerge.

... Every policy shift over the past year has corresponded to a peak in a certain asset class: the dovish rate cut on October 29th last year corresponded to a Bitcoin peak; Trump's nomination of Warsh on January 30th this year corresponded to a gold peak; Warsh's dovish misstep at the FOMC on June 17th corresponded to semiconductor and South Korean KOSPI peaks; and the hawkish rate hike on September 16th corresponded to a copper price peak, a low investment-grade spread, and the starting point of a dollar rally. Conversely, the signal that the rate hike panic has peaked is a mirror image of the above trends: the dollar peaks, while Bitcoin, gold, and KOSPI bottom out. The current situation is that all four conditions have failed to materialize—the US dollar recorded its strongest weekly close since April 2025, Bitcoin fell for the seventh consecutive week, gold returned to September 2025 levels, and the KOSPI fell below 5,000 points. The only sign of a turnaround was that safe-haven funds began shifting from the US dollar to the Japanese yen last Friday. $310 billion in bargain hunting, 3% betting on a hard landing. Hartnett's second key word this week is "clearing event"—he is clearly impatient with the overuse of this term. His position data precisely explains why: without clearing, there is no clearing event. A Bank of America November fund manager survey showed that only 3% of investors expected a "hard landing," 50% expected a "soft landing," and 42% expected a "no landing." Cash positions were at an extremely low level of 3.6%. Asset allocations were long on stocks and short on bonds. A record $310 billion flowed into equity funds and ETFs over the past four weeks. Hartnett concluded that prices have capitulated, but positions have not, and a full buy signal is not advisable until the latter occurs. Disagreements do exist. Goldman Sachs Prime ledgers show that hedge fund net leverage is at its lowest level in over five years, below the lows of "Liberation Day," with tech stock selling at its fastest pace in a decade and individual stock short selling at its largest scale since June 2022. However, hedge funds are not the main holders—ETFs are bearing the losses, and ETF investors were still buying into the decline in AI stocks last week. The Bank of America Bull & Bear Index fell from 7.4 to 7.1 due to significant outflows from emerging market and junk bonds, widening spreads between high-yield and bank subordinated bonds, deteriorating market breadth, and a shift to short positions in futures. The index remains closer to "sell" than "panic": global market breadth is at the 18th percentile, equity flows are at the 99th percentile, and fund manager positions are fixed at the 100th percentile. The bond market lacks a pressure relief valve: long-term bonds may see negative returns for the sixth consecutive year. During this sell-off, bonds failed to provide a buffer for most of the time. Hartnett points out that 30-year US Treasury bonds are heading for their sixth consecutive year of negative price returns, the longest streak since the Vietnam War (1963-1969). As of the time of writing, the 30-year Treasury yield was only 25 basis points away from its recent high, while the Nasdaq had fallen 15%, bank stocks 16%, and crude oil 22%. His core concern is that the risk of yields rising rather than falling is greater in the next recession due to excessively high debt levels. Last Friday, the 30-year Treasury yield closed at 5.31%, down 18 basis points for the week, seemingly opening a crack in the pressure relief valve. Citadel Securities believes there is a record 3.5 standard deviation gap between yields and growth. However, there is tension within Hartnett's notes: the first page states that the risk of rising yields is greatest in a recession, while the hard landing scenario on the third page begins with allocators buying bonds; and last week he also said that no one wants to touch Treasuries until yields reach 5.5% to 6.5%—these three cannot be true simultaneously.

Soft Landing Scenario: Below 7,000 Points is the Buying Point

Hartnett's soft landing path is: if inflation falls before spring, employment stabilizes, productivity gains are confirmed, and earnings growth remains above 10%, then below 7,000 points on the S&P 500 is the buying point—last Friday's close was 75 points below that level. At that time, the "broad bull market" will restart, and sectors that have not participated in the AI ​​rally will no longer be expensive: the equal-weighted S&P 500's P/E ratio is 16, mid-cap stocks are 15 (30-year average 16), and non-US stocks are 12 (average 13).

The order is equally important. His advice is to first preserve capital, wait for the panic to become apparent, and wait for the narrative to shift from interest rate hikes to interest rate cuts before buying cyclical "Cs": cryptocurrencies, chips, copper, consumer goods, and apartment real estate.

Valuation matrices show that the S&P 7,338 points corresponds to 18 times the forward earnings per share of $408, implying 16% earnings growth, close to market consensus. Last Friday's 6,925 points correspond to 17 times, or 17.9 times based on a 10% growth to $387. If earnings only grow by 5% ($370) and a 16 times valuation is applied, the matrix gives a target of 5,913 points; Goldman Sachs' Brian Garrett believes that if the fourth quarter of 2018 is completely repeated, the endpoint would be 6,294 points, exactly 17 times the same earnings. Two institutions, two methods, and the worst-case scenario points are highly similar. Hard landing scenario: From "boom cycle" to "doomsday cycle" Hartnett is betting on the worst-case scenario. He believes the probability of a "hard landing" is underestimated, and the market's consensus expectations for "prosperity" are too high—nominal GDP growth of 5% to 6% and earnings per share growth of over 15% in 2027—both of which rely on two weakening pillars. The first is household stock wealth, which has shrunk by about $5 trillion since the last quarter, although it will still increase by about $8 trillion for the whole year. However, the S&P 500's market capitalization evaporated by about $1.3 trillion in just one day last Thursday. The second is AI capital expenditure: hyperscale cloud vendors' capital expenditure is expected to reach $1.3 trillion in 2027, higher than this year's $822 billion and 2025's $412 billion, while their total free cash flow will turn from a positive $191 billion in 2025 to a negative $61 billion this year, and further decline to a negative $283 billion next year. This gap necessitates financing, which explains the market tensions of the past two weeks: the largest IPO in history nearly reached its offering price on its second day of trading; SpaceX managed to pay $47 billion for Nvidia chips without borrowing; Blackstone's data center subsidiary failed to sell an $800 million investment-grade bond; and the entire ecosystem's "lender of last resort" indicated it would significantly raise financing thresholds. Hartnett states that voters, the bond market, and asset allocators are sending the same signal: slow down data center construction. Voters expressed their opinions on November 3rd, allocators gave a record percentage of "overinvestment" in surveys, and the bond market has been under pressure since September. Two indicators confirming a hard landing have remained unchanged: initial jobless claims exceeding 250,000 and investment-grade spreads exceeding 100 basis points. If triggered, the "boom cycle" (rising stock prices, rising wealth, rising spending, rising capital expenditures, and further rising stock prices) will turn into a "doomsday cycle," forcing investors to reduce their stock holdings and increase their holdings of bonds, Chinese assets (with ample fiscal space), the US dollar, and assets negatively correlated with AI, such as REITs and real estate. His summary is "more apartments, less chips." In other words, a hard landing trade would reverse the four major trades that defined the 2020s: buy everything except bonds (30-year US Treasury yields -62% at peak and trough), buy everything except China (Chinese stocks have fallen an average of 5% annually over the past decade, the worst performing globally), buy everything except the US dollar (Bitcoin and gold have seen compound annual growth rates of 44% and 23% respectively, peaking in October 2025 and January 2026), and bet everything on AI (Nasdaq market capitalization has increased by $26 trillion since March 2023). One of these has already clearly reversed, the second began on October 6th, and the third started to loosen after the bond rebound. Concentration risk remains: the top ten AI stocks still account for 38% of the US market, on par with the "Nifty Fifty" (40%), Japan's (44%), and the TMT sector during the dot-com bubble (41%), but far lower than the 63% of the railroad era. The 2000 scenario: Twelve rallies during a bear market. While most on Wall Street are looking to 2018, Hartnett is looking back at an earlier cycle. He writes that the market was trading the "bubble" in May and is now trading the "post-bubble." The path in 2000 was: tech stocks peaked in March, the Fed still raised rates by 100 basis points that year, and then the market spread to "boring sectors"—consumer staples, utilities, financials, and healthcare rose 40% to 60%, while tech stocks nearly halved. This is highly similar to the trend since the summer of 2026. What hasn't yet happened is 2001: interest rate hikes caught up with the economy, safe havens failed, and utilities, the hero of 2000, became the worst-performing sector in 2001. Two details are worth noting: the US dollar was strong in both 2000 and 2001; the Nasdaq saw twelve rebounds exceeding 10% during its decline, including one at 35% and two exceeding 40%. This is a necessary reminder for investors waiting for the broadening rules to trigger and then buying on the rebound. The third detail directly corresponds to Hartnett's two questions: the last rate hike in that cycle was in May 2000, and the Fed cut rates by 475 basis points throughout 2001. The answer to "when will the rate hikes end?" is "soon"; but the answer to "whether it will end before the recession" is no. In the 2018 version, Powell raised rates in December, bottomed out before Christmas, and reversed course in the first week of January; in the 2000 version, the Fed stopped early, and the bear market still lasted two years due to profit issues. The difference between the two is the difference between position accidents and capital expenditure collapses. Fund Flows: Stocks attracted $66.6 billion, bonds saw outflows for the first time since April 2025. In the week ending last Wednesday (covering Nvidia's earnings and pre-IPO cash raising, but excluding Anthropic's listing and two worst trading days), investors poured $66.6 billion into stocks (ETFs saw $73.5 billion inflows, mutual funds saw $6.8 billion outflows), cash inflows were $400 million, and gold saw $200 million inflows; cryptocurrencies saw $1.1 billion outflows, and bonds saw $7.4 billion outflows. In fixed income, bank loans continued to be favored, aligning with the allocation logic of investors who still believe in interest rate hikes; emerging market bonds saw an outflow of over 1% of assets within a week. Looking at the full year, 2026 is expected to see record inflows in several areas: global equities $1.5 trillion (annualized), global bonds $909 billion, US equities $751 billion, US large-cap stocks $669 billion, investment-grade bonds $443 billion, US Treasuries $243 billion, technology funds $229 billion, and South Korean funds $79 billion; while consumer funds will see a record outflow of $20 billion. How do investors with a 3.6% cash position view 2027? A survey shows that fund managers anticipate a soft landing, declining inflation, and slower growth in AI capital expenditures. Entering 2027, they are overweighting equities, commodities, emerging markets, healthcare, and industrials, and underweighting cash, bonds, REITs, consumer goods, and energy. The best asset classes are international equities (36%) and US equities (24%), the best indices are the Nasdaq and MSCI Emerging Markets (21% each), and the best currency is the Japanese yen (42%). Their year-end 2027 targets are: 10-year US Treasury yield 4.9%, euro/dollar 1.12, S&P 500 7,926 points, and gold $4,341. The first target was achieved thirteen months ahead of schedule last Friday. The S&P 500 target is 14% higher than the current price, and the gold target is 24% higher. For contrarian investors, Hartnett lists the effective pairings for 2026: long crude oil, short cryptocurrency; long energy, short consumer discretionary; long semiconductors, short telecom; long small-cap value, short large-cap growth; long Taiwan, short China; long cybersecurity, short defense. Annual themes include: war over peace, rate hikes over rate cuts, greed over fear, AI bond issuance over AI unemployment, concentration over breadth, and IPOs over buybacks in a week with $107 billion in issuance. If these trades reverse in 2027, fear, breadth, and buybacks will return. The suspense beyond 80 points: Hartnett has adhered to a principle for over a decade: the market stops panicking only when policymakers start to panic. This week's notes put a price on this principle—6,845 points for the S&P 500 and 80 basis points for the IG CDX. The former only requires a bad Monday. The market has partially completed the thinking for the Fed: the 50-basis-point rate hike has been moved out of the question, expectations for a December rate cut have faded, and the 10-year yield has fallen below 5%. However, the disagreement lies in whether 6,845 points is the end. A Fed that has failed to meet its inflation target for 67 consecutive months, has three overheated CPI reports on its desk, and has just seen voters punish the ruling party for price inflation, is unlikely to stop simply because the S&P 500 saw zero growth for the year. Cook's statement last Friday proves this. A 20% drop was needed in 2018, when there was no inflation problem. This week's figure is $310 billion: the largest inflow into equity funds in four weeks, from investors with 3.6% cash positions and only 3% anticipating a hard landing. Wall Street is waiting for a liquidation, and $310 billion shows that no one has completed the liquidation. Hartnett will release the next Flow Show on December 3rd. The market will then know whether the Federal Reserve still favors Wall Street.

data.title: A South Korean business partner is offering $150 million to bail out a company in which Trump's son has invested that owes unpaid wages.
data.description:
Author: Zen, PANews

South Korean conglomerate Base Group is considering investing $150 million in Foundation Future Industries (hereinafter referred to as Foundation), a US military robot manufacturer.

Foundation has only raised about $11 million in total funding so far, making this a considerable investment. Prior to this potential investment being revealed, Foundation was embroiled in controversy over unpaid employee wages, and its founder was reported to have borrowed $4.6 million from the company to purchase a luxury mansion.

Even more noteworthy is the presence of a special investor behind Foundation—Eric Trump, the second son of US President Donald Trump.

He not only invested in the robotics company but also serves as its chief strategic advisor. Base Group, the South Korean conglomerate preparing to invest $150 million, happens to be a long-time business partner of the Trump family.

Judging from the relationship between the two parties, Eric Trump likely played a facilitating role in this potential investment. Base Group and the Trump family have maintained a business relationship for nearly a decade, with collaborations covering wine trading and golf course development. Previously, Base Group's payment of $2 million to Trump-related companies sparked questions from Democratic senators regarding potential improper transfer of benefits. A financially troubled robotics company, a controversial founder, and South Korean capital with close ties to the Trump family together form the more complex story behind this potential investment. From the bankruptcy of the financial company Synapse to Foundation's unpaid wages, before founding Foundation, Sankaet Pathak was a prominent entrepreneur in the US fintech industry. In 2014, he co-founded Synapse, initially aiming to provide digital banking services to those underserved by traditional banks. It later transformed into a Bank as a Service (BaaS) infrastructure platform. Its business model involves providing technical interfaces to fintech companies without banking licenses, helping them connect to licensed banks and conduct account management, deposit, payment, and debit card services. This model coincided with the rapid development of the US fintech industry. In 2019, Synapse completed a $33 million Series B funding round led by a16z, bringing its total funding to over $50 million. Its clients include well-known fintech companies such as digital bank Dave, corporate finance platform Mercury, and savings app Yotta. According to Synapse, in 2022, its platform covered 18 million end users, with an annualized transaction volume of approximately $76 billion. Pathak thus became a star among Silicon Valley fintech startups. However, along with its rapid expansion, Pathak's management style also sparked controversy. In April 2020, Forbes published an investigative report, interviewing 13 current and former employees and 6 customers, revealing internal management problems at Synapse. Several former employees accused the company of unstable technical systems, poor code quality, and a harsh management style. These management problems, at the time, had not yet escalated into a full-blown business crisis. But as the company's business expanded, weaknesses in its technical systems and internal management gradually became apparent. In 2023, Synapse's relationship with partner banks broke down, and it lost important clients, ultimately plunging the fintech company into difficulties. In 2023, Synapse clashed violently with its main partner bank, Evolve Bank & Trust. Subsequently, Mercury, a major client that contributed approximately 60% of Synapse's revenue at its peak, decided to bypass Synapse and partner directly with Evolve. Synapse's operations deteriorated rapidly, and the company laid off about 40% of its staff in October 2023. More seriously, Synapse and Evolve began blaming each other for approximately $13 million in discrepancies in customer funds accounts. As the investigation deepened, the funding gap widened. In April 2024, Synapse filed for bankruptcy protection, and the customer funds problems erupted. Due to a significant discrepancy between the user accounts maintained by Synapse and the actual funds held by its partner banks, many consumers were unable to withdraw their deposits, with the affected funds exceeding $200 million at one point. The bankruptcy trustee estimates a shortfall of approximately $65 million to $95 million between the balance due to customers and the funds actually held by the bank. The Synapse bankruptcy case has also attracted the attention of the US Department of Justice. Federal prosecutors in New York have convened a grand jury to investigate potential criminal offenses such as accounting fraud and wire fraud behind the Synapse customer funding shortfall and have subpoenaed the company's former CFO. As of now, this criminal investigation has not yet reached a publicly released final conclusion. While Synapse was bankrupt and the customer funding issue remained unresolved, Pathak had already turned to the then-highly sought-after field of embodied intelligence, embarking on his next entrepreneurial venture. In 2024, Pathak founded the robotics company Foundation, dedicated to developing humanoid robots for industrial and military applications, and quickly secured approximately $11 million in early-stage funding from investors such as Tribe Capital. However, the new venture soon encountered financial disputes as well. On November 14, 2026, CNBC reported that Foundation had been in arrears on some employee salaries since October. Meanwhile, Pathak had borrowed $4.6 million from the company in 2025 to purchase a home in California. CNBC also pointed out that Pathak is Foundation's sole board member, wielding highly centralized corporate governance power. In response to the allegations, Pathak stated that the loan agreement was reached in August 2025 and was unrelated to the company's current cash flow difficulties. In an email to employees on November 8, Pathak attributed the salary arrears to issues with the timing of financing. He stated that considering the progress of the investment with South Korea's Base Group, the company was only facing a question of when the funds would arrive, not a survival crisis. Four days later, in another email, he revealed that the two parties planned to establish a long-term partnership, with business also involving the supply of aluminum for robots and lithium for batteries. For this robotics startup, only two years old, the pending funding has become a vital hope for maintaining daily operations. Exaggerated Claims Beneath the Military Robot Narrative: Looking only at Foundation's business promotions, it's hard to associate it with a company that can't even pay its employees on time. Compared to humanoid robot companies primarily targeting industrial and domestic applications, Foundation has increasingly focused on military applications in recent years, actively promoting the prospects of robots in reconnaissance, logistics, and battlefield operations. In 2024, Foundation acquired humanoid robot company Boardwalk Robotics, gaining access to related technology and R&D teams, and subsequently launched the Phantom series of robots. The company hopes to leverage the bipedal mobility of humanoid robots to enable them to enter factories, construction sites, and complex environments where traditional wheeled robots struggle, including battlefield reconnaissance, hazardous area inspection, and military logistics. In early 2026, Eric Trump became an investor in Foundation and began serving as its Chief Strategic Advisor. With Eric Trump's support and endorsement, Foundation's vision for military robots began to gain more attention. In April of this year, Eric Trump appeared on Fox Business with Pathak to publicly promote Foundation's humanoid robot project. Eric Trump stated that his investment was intended to help the United States gain a leading position in the humanoid robot field. During the program, the host also mentioned that Foundation had secured a $24 million Pentagon contract. However, this claim was later investigated and questioned by several media outlets. In July, Wired's investigation found that the government contract documents provided by Foundation primarily came from its acquisition of Boardwalk Robotics and its collaboration with the Institute for Human and Machine Cognition (IHMC). The San Francisco Standard further reviewed federal procurement records and found that Boardwalk had previously secured four contracts totaling approximately $3.22 million, while another U.S. Navy contract worth approximately $24.8 million was actually awarded to IHMC. In fact, Foundation's commercial claims had already sparked controversy as early as 2024. At that time, the company claimed in its financing materials that General Motors might become its first customer, with potential purchase orders reaching $300 million. However, General Motors subsequently publicly denied the partnership and accused Foundation of fabricating its claims. Foundation co-founder Mike LeBlanc later admitted that the funding materials exaggerated the relationship between the two parties. A similar information gap exists in military applications. Foundation had claimed that its robots were already being tested in Ukraine and proposed future use for reconnaissance, mine clearance, and battlefield operations. However, in November of this year, the San Francisco Standard, citing journalists involved in the trip and the Ukrainian defense technology organization Brave1, pointed out that the Foundation team did not enter Ukraine at that time, nor did they complete the previously hinted field demonstrations. On November 18, Foundation released its second-generation humanoid robot, the Phantom MKII, along with its accompanying Cortex II artificial intelligence system. Foundation claims that the Phantom MKII can carry a load of 200 pounds (approximately 91 kg) while walking and can adapt to complex environments such as rain, snow, and dust, with a maximum endurance of up to 6 hours. The company plans to start production in early 2027 and gradually expand production capacity. Behind the $150 Million Investment: Trump Family Connections

Compared to the financial disputes surrounding the Foundation's founders, the background of South Korean company Base Group's potential investment is equally noteworthy.

Base Group's businesses span industries such as construction, aluminum processing, and wine, but it has never been known for investing in robotics or AI technologies.

This South Korean conglomerate's business ties with the Trump family date back to at least 2017. That year, a Base Group subsidiary reached an agreement with Trump Winery to import and sell Trump-branded wines in South Korea. Since then, business dealings between the two parties have gradually increased.

In January 2025, Base Group Chairman Kim Seong-jip attended Trump's second presidential inauguration and maintained contact with members of the Trump family.

In February 2026, Base Group invited Eric Trump to visit Seoul to participate in an event discussing South Korea-US business cooperation. In August, the Trump Organization further announced a partnership with Base Group to develop a golf course in South Korea. However, the business relationship between the two parties also attracted the attention of the US Congress in the same year. According to Trump's 2025 financial disclosure documents, Base Group paid $2 million to Trump-related companies. The funds were explained as non-refundable development costs related to a golf course project in South Korea. However, the timing of the payment raised suspicions among some Democratic lawmakers in the United States. This is because Base Group's affiliated company, Korea Aluminium, was previously involved in a U.S. Department of Commerce investigation into tariff evasion related to aluminum products. On August 6, 2026, Democratic Senators Elizabeth Warren, Richard Blumenthal, and Andy Kim jointly wrote to Base Group, demanding an explanation of the specific background of the $2 million payment and whether the group had discussed relevant trade policies with the Trump family. Now, Base Group is preparing to invest another $150 million in a company affiliated with the Trump family, naturally bringing their business relationship back into focus. However, on the one hand, Base Group's previous business dealings with the Trump family have already been questioned by Democratic senators; on the other hand, the Foundation's involvement in military robotics raises concerns that potential foreign investment could trigger national security reviews. For Foundation, already mired in unpaid wages, a potential $150 million investment could alleviate its immediate financial pressure. However, the founder's past management controversies, the unproven commercialization capabilities of its robots, and its close business ties with the Trump family also introduce considerable uncertainty into the deal.

data.title: What is the future of US control over computing power in China after the Huang Renxun incident?
data.description:
Author: ThinkTank, ShanghaiTech University

On November 12, 2026, Jensen Huang, co-founder of Nvidia who had led the company for 33 years, resigned from his positions as president, CEO, and director. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was appointed interim CEO, and senior director Harvey C. Jones became the company's first chairman of the board. The immediate trigger for this personnel change was the New York Times' continuous disclosure, starting in late October, of Huang's private dealings with former executives of Singaporean cloud computing service provider Megaspeed, as well as a counterintelligence investigation by US intelligence agencies. Coupled with internal disputes over executive relationships, Nvidia's market capitalization fell by more than $600 billion within two weeks of the news breaking.

From a purely corporate governance perspective, this appears to be a strategic departure by a senior executive to mitigate compliance risks. However, within the framework of the global semiconductor industry and the technological competition between major powers, Huang's departure removes the most crucial coordinating link that has existed for the past four years between hardliners on US national security and the supply of cross-border commercial computing power. Since the US tightened semiconductor export controls in 2022, the reason why a certain degree of commercial buffer has been maintained in the computing power field between China and the US is largely due to the dual arrangements spearheaded by Huang. On the industry side, he leveraged Nvidia's abundant cash flow and off-balance-sheet guarantees totaling $530 billion to provide credit backing for emerging global cloud computing service providers, maintaining a massive third-party computing power leasing market. On the policy side, he consistently emphasized to Washington policymakers the commercial value of maintaining Chinese AI developers' dependence on the US software ecosystem, creating a realistic space for the sale of downgraded chips to China and the leasing of remote computing power in overseas data centers. With Huang's resignation under pressure from national security accountability, coupled with the Democratic Party's potential regaining control of both houses of Congress in the November 2026 midterm elections, US control over computing power from China is shifting from executive branch regulations with negotiating flexibility to congressional-led codified laws. Just four days after Huang's departure, on November 16th, the US Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) released the Interim Final Rule on "Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors," initially including Chinese companies leasing advanced computing power overseas and access to chips from five countries including Singapore and Malaysia in the licensing review process. The next phase of regulation will simultaneously tighten controls in four areas: cloud-based remote access permits, chip-embedded location verification, alignment of export of allied devices, and pre-approval by Congress. The hardening of external regulatory mechanisms will profoundly change the resource allocation methods of China's artificial intelligence industry. In the short term, the compliance clearing of offshore computing power leasing channels in Southeast Asia and the Middle East will increase the cost for domestic cutting-edge large-scale model teams to acquire large-scale training clusters, prompting a further concentration of R&D focus on sparse architectures and single-time word generation efficiency. In the medium to long term, the narrowing of external computing power acquisition channels eliminates the expectation of leading domestic institutions continuing to wait and see about US hardware supply, driving core algorithm engineering forces to shift to domestic computing power systems to complete joint software and hardware iterations. At the same time, the past collaborative relationship between Chinese and American engineers in jointly optimizing global open-source inference frameworks around general-purpose graphics processors will also weaken, and the prospect of global computing power infrastructure gradually evolving into two related but independently evolving technological systems is becoming increasingly clear. Chapter 1: Changes in the Political and Business Structure Behind Nvidia's Power Shift 1.1 Counterintelligence Review Triggers Management Change at Nvidia Among large technology companies with a market capitalization exceeding four trillion US dollars, Nvidia has long maintained a distinct founder-led characteristic, with product roadmap decisions, securing core supply chain contracts, and mediating government relations all highly concentrated in the hands of Jensen Huang. On November 8, 2026, when Nvidia's board of directors announced an independent investigation into allegations of personal relationships among executives exposed by the media, the statement still emphasized confidence in Huang and his management team; however, only three days later, on November 11, the board formally accepted his resignation, effective immediately. The core factor that prompted the board to change its attitude in such a short time was not simply an internal ethical dispute, but rather the national security accountability risk arising from the intertwining of personal scandals and investigations into the cross-border flow of computing power. The core party involved in this dispute, Singaporean data center operator Megaspeed International, was spun off from a Chinese gaming company and restructured in 2023 to become an official cloud partner of NVIDIA. Between 2023 and 2025, it cumulatively purchased at least $4.6 billion worth of NVIDIA hardware, building computing clusters in Southeast Asia and leasing computing power to clients including large Chinese technology companies. Although China has explicitly refuted claims that the individuals involved have intelligence backgrounds, and the company has denied any illegal physical transfer of chips, estimates based on global accelerator shipment and power consumption models from research institutions show that a considerable amount of restricted NVIDIA chips have entered the Chinese market through various channels in recent years. With the US Department of Justice, the FBI, and relevant congressional committees simultaneously investigating, if the founder remains in office, Nvidia will not only face lengthy congressional hearings, but its export license approvals for global markets may also be subject to administrative freeze. The appointment of Kress, who has long been responsible for financial compliance, as interim CEO and the creation of an independent chairman position are essentially defensive institutional arrangements adopted by the board of directors to isolate itself from political and regulatory shocks. 1.2 Founder's Credit Deterioration Tightens Global Computing Power Financing Chain The direct impact of Huang Renxun's departure on the global computing power supply structure is primarily reflected in the weakening of Nvidia's function as an industry credit intermediary. Internally, Nvidia previously had approximately 60 executives reporting directly to Huang Renxun. The company neither had a conventional second-in-command nor was it heavily constrained by short-term financial ratios. Based on this decision-making mechanism, Huang Renxun transformed Nvidia's massive free cash flow and balance sheet into financing leverage for the expansion of downstream computing power infrastructure. According to Nvidia's Q2 FY2027 financial report, the company's total off-balance-sheet guarantees have increased significantly from $184 billion in the previous quarter to $530 billion. This includes a $36 billion "take-or-pay" capacity guarantee agreement for emerging cloud computing service providers, and approximately $99 billion in equity investments across the industry chain. From a financial perspective, this set of off-balance-sheet commitments is equivalent to Nvidia using its own credit to enhance the creditworthiness of its downstream customers. Many emerging cloud computing service providers and startups, lacking investment-grade ratings, are able to raise funds from the debt market at lower interest rates thanks to minimum rental guarantees or data center lease guarantees provided by Nvidia, which then flow back to purchase Nvidia's high-margin hardware. On the upstream manufacturing side, Nvidia's quarterly supply chain and capacity procurement commitments also increased from $119 billion to $279 billion, mainly invested in high-bandwidth memory and advanced packaging capacity. Through Huang Renxun's long-term direct cooperation with South Korean memory manufacturers and Taiwanese foundry executives, Nvidia was able to secure priority quotas and obtain procurement quotes that were about 20% lower than its competitors. With professional managers taking over the reins, the company's governance focus naturally shifts towards risk control, cash flow security, and stock buybacks. Previously, Kress had taken a cautious approach to high-risk guarantee schemes for ultra-large-scale customers in internal decision-making. In the future, Nvidia's credit guarantee standards for emerging overseas computing cloud providers will inevitably become stricter, and small and medium-sized computing operators that heavily rely on cash flow from Asian cross-border customers will be the first to face financing contraction pressure. 1.3 Washington's Moderate Business Faction Loses Core Policy Pivot Beyond corporate restructuring, Huang Renxun's departure has disrupted the internal checks and balances formed in Washington regarding its chip policy towards China. Over the past four years, two distinct approaches have emerged within the US policy community regarding computing power to China: Bipartisan security hardliners in Congress advocate for strict physical isolation of advanced computing power to prevent any cutting-edge chips or computing services from flowing to China; while industry forces, represented by Jensen Huang, have repeatedly argued to the administration that moderately retaining compliant, reduced chip exports and overseas cloud computing services would keep China's AI R&D system within the US-based hardware and software architecture, thereby reducing the commercial incentive for Chinese companies to fully invest in domestically produced alternative chips. During the first half of the Trump administration's second term, this business logic gained considerable traction within the White House and the Department of Commerce. Officials, led by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, favored including chip licensing in bilateral trade negotiations. The US government not only revoked the previous administration's global AI proliferation classification restrictions in 2025, but also allowed Nvidia to apply for sales of some high-performance chips to China on a case-by-case basis in 2026, provided it paid a 25% revenue share. Simultaneously, it shelved several additional licensing rules and entity list additions for Southeast Asian data centers. However, with Jensen Huang's resignation due to compliance controversies related to China, Nvidia's policy lobbying credibility in Washington was severely damaged. The Treasury Department and congressional hardliners subsequently publicly criticized the Commerce Department for being too lenient in export enforcement. US hyperscale cloud providers like Microsoft and Amazon, who already supported restricting competitors' overseas chip sales, gained a more favorable position in policy discussions. With the strongest voices from industry opposing a complete ban fading, moderates within the administration advocating for policy flexibility found it difficult to prevent a comprehensive tightening of regulations. Chapter Two: Legislative Shift in US Export Controls Following the Midterm Elections 2.1 Change of Control in Both Houses Clears Backlogged Bills The management shake-up at Nvidia coincided with the conclusion of the US midterm elections in November 2026, and the overlapping political cycles further amplified the certainty of a policy shift. As of mid-November, vote counts showed that the Democrats won over 250 seats in the House of Representatives and at least 54 seats in the Senate, and will take full control of the legislative agendas of both houses and the chair positions of key committees when the 120th Congress opens in January 2027. On the issue of US technology controls on China, the two parties are largely aligned. The reason why many previous bills restricting chip and cloud computing power have been delayed in completing the legislative process is mainly due to the internal congressional agenda scheduling and cross-issue political games, rather than disagreements on the controls themselves.

Looking back at mid-2026, when the Senate was drafting amendments to the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (NDAA), it planned to include four bills related to the regulation of Chinese-made chips and cloud computing power. However, due to Democratic senators' dissatisfaction with the White House's unauthorized military actions in the Middle East and the increase in defense spending, they voted against it in the procedural vote in July, causing the bill to receive only 50 votes in support and fail to reach the 60-vote threshold required to conclude the debate. After the midterm election results were announced and the Nvidia incident unfolded, two clear time windows emerged for legislative progress.

... The first window of opportunity is the "lame duck" congressional session from November to December 2026, when the heads of the Senate and House Armed Services Committees and the Foreign Affairs Committee are finalizing the National Defense Authorization Act, striving to retain the chip control provisions with high consensus in the final version before the end-of-year recess. The second window of opportunity is after the new Congress takes office in January 2027, when Chuck Schumer is expected to return to the Senate Majority Leader position, and Elizabeth Warren, a long-time advocate for strict chip export controls, is expected to become the chair of the Senate Banking Committee, which has export control jurisdiction. Even if some provisions fail to pass under the National Defense Act by the end of the year, they will receive priority scheduling and be quickly passed as separate legislation next year. 2.2 Shift of Regulatory Leadership from Executive Discretion to Congressional Legislation The most significant institutional feature of the next stage of US control over China's computing power is the shift of rule-making power from executive department regulations to written law in Congress. Under the existing system, the specific technical parameters and licensing policies for U.S. export controls are primarily implemented by the Bureau of Industry and Security of the Department of Commerce through amendments to the Export Administration Regulations. This executive-led model grants the President and the Secretary of Commerce considerable discretion, allowing them to flexibly adjust approval standards based on changes in macroeconomic and trade relations. For example, in the trade negotiations between the U.S. and China in the second half of 2026 regarding the extension of the trade agreement and the procurement of key minerals and agricultural products, relaxing or tightening export licenses for specific chips has always been a negotiating tool in the hands of the U.S. negotiating team. A series of bills being pushed forward by Congress are intended to compress the discretionary space of the executive branch in the field of national security technologies. The most representative of these, the AI ​​Oversight Act, explicitly proposes to incorporate the approval process for exporting advanced artificial intelligence chips to countries of concern into a congressional oversight framework similar to that for foreign arms sales. It not only requires the revocation of existing relevant export licenses but also stipulates that the Department of Commerce must submit applications for congressional review before issuing specific licenses and cannot arbitrarily lower the technical thresholds for controlled chips within two years. Faced with the impending change of control in Congress and the public pressure stemming from the Nvidia incident, the White House has recently shifted its previously passive stance on legislation limiting its discretionary power, instead providing specific technical revisions to congressional committees. For the White House, proactively participating in legislative coordination prevents bill provisions from excessively encroaching on diplomatic authority and allows it to leverage strong congressional legislation as an external constraint in bilateral trade negotiations. Once core computing power restrictions are elevated from administrative regulations to congressional law, even if bilateral trade relations ease temporarily, the US administration will find it difficult to unilaterally loosen restrictions on computing power exports.

Chapter 3 The Evolution of Four Mechanisms for the Next Stage of Control over Computing Power from China

3.1 The Remote Access Security Act Includes Cloud Computing Power in Export Licensing

In terms of specific control tools, the Remote Access Security Act (RASA, H.R. 2683) has the most profound impact on the existing cross-border computing power business model. This bill was passed by the House of Representatives in January 2026 with 369 votes in favor and 22 against, and is currently awaiting approval from the Senate Banking Committee or integration into the defense bill.

For nearly two decades, US export controls have followed the traditional principle of physical cross-border transactions: as long as servers equipped with high-end accelerator cards are actually deployed in data centers in Singapore, Malaysia, the Middle East, or Europe, and there is no physical transfer of the hardware, Chinese companies remotely renting these servers to train models does not constitute an "export" activity requiring a license under current regulations. From the perspective of economic interests and security monitoring, this operation, similar to an "offshore dollar market," was originally quite advantageous to the US: computing power rental income belonged to US chip manufacturers and overseas cloud operators, the physical control of the servers remained overseas, allowing for the ability to disconnect the network at any time, and also allowing for some control over the scale of customer computing power usage. However, after cases like Megaspeed were exposed, the US Congress generally believed that offshore cloud leasing had become a major channel for circumventing the physical chip ban. The RASA Act, through amendments to the Export Control Reform Act, formally authorized the Bureau of Industry and Security of the Department of Commerce to implement licensing management for remote cloud access to controlled items and required cloud computing service providers to establish customer identity verification systems similar to those used by financial institutions for anti-money laundering compliance. This means that the regulatory boundaries extend from traditional customs inspection of physical goods to the level of network accounts and computing power allocation in global data centers. Once the bill takes effect, emerging cloud computing providers across the Asia-Pacific, Middle East, and Europe and the United States will face secondary sanctions and supply disruptions if they continue to provide remote computing power for cutting-edge chips to unlicensed Chinese entities. While Congress is advancing the legislation, the executive branch has already issued the Provisional Final Rule on Responding to Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors on November 16, 2026, adding Articles 744.24 and 742.6 of the Export Administration Regulations and formally repealing the old Artificial Intelligence Propagation Framework. The new regulations stipulate that any data center globally (including networked data centers sharing underlying resources) must obtain prior case-by-case permission before providing advanced computing power exceeding 12 million aggregate total processing power (TPP) to enterprises headquartered or ultimately headquartered in mainland China and Macau (including those provided through third-country subsidiaries or third-party intermediaries). Existing compliant services must obtain formal permission within 90 days of the rules taking effect, with only purely commercial recommendation systems (excluding any generative models) being specifically excluded. Furthermore, the new regulations introduce export licenses for advanced computing items in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil (US-owned parent companies can be exempted from territorial licenses based on monthly reports, but the allocation of computing power to China is still subject to usage review), and tighten the pathway for front-end wafer foundries and packaging and testing companies to overturn the presumption of chip classification for unapproved designers.

3.2 Chip Security Act Promotes Mandatory Verification of Hardware Location

In response to the gray market trade chain of dismantling and transferring physical servers through intermediaries in third countries, the US Congress simultaneously introduced the Chip Security Act (S. 1705 / H.R. 3447), which was unanimously approved by the House Foreign Affairs Committee with a vote of 42 to 0. In the past few years, although US law enforcement agencies have investigated and dealt with many cases of illegal transfers—for example, in March 2026, the US Department of Justice filed a prosecution in a case involving the illegal transfer of approximately $2.5 billion worth of Nvidia chip servers—the cost of law enforcement by manually tracking the global multi-level distribution network is extremely high, making it difficult to fundamentally block the flow of hardware.

The proposed "Chip Security Act" addresses this by integrating enforcement and oversight into the chip hardware architecture. It mandates that all exported advanced AI chips and servers incorporate tamper-proof location verification technology and requires license holders to immediately report any deviations from approved locations or signs of tampering to the Department of Commerce. In engineering terms, this location verification relies on the chip's built-in hardware security keys and network communication latency calculations: accelerator cards in operation periodically communicate encrypted with designated verification nodes, determining the server's geographical location based on the physical transmission latency of optical signals in fiber optic cables. Nvidia had previously launched a data center management telemetry tool called "Fleet Intelligence," capable of monitoring cluster performance metrics and physical location, but it was previously only available voluntarily to cloud partners applying for official certification. The new legislation effectively transforms this voluntary commercial tool into a legally mandated condition for shipment, ensuring compliance verification throughout the entire chip lifecycle, from factory activation to daily operation, significantly raising the technical barrier to obtaining large-scale, usable clusters through physical smuggling. 3.3 Multilateral Equipment Coordination Act Tightens Restrictions on Upstream Production Line Expansion In addition to blocking overseas cloud leasing and physical chip transshipment, the AI ​​Oversight Act and the Multilateral Coordination Act on Hardware Technology Regulation (MATCH Act, S. 4281) tightened constraints on both finished chip quotas and upstream manufacturing equipment. The AI ​​Oversight Act requires that advanced computing chips prioritize the needs of the U.S. domestic market, abolish existing licenses for countries of concern, and prevent chip companies from designing products specifically for restricted markets through rigorous congressional review. The Multilateral Coordination Act on Hardware Technology Regulation focuses on the unification of multilateral rules for semiconductor manufacturing equipment.
