For some time, due to the stricter unilateral regulations imposed by the United States compared to those of its allies, Dutch and Japanese equipment manufacturers were still able to sell certain deep ultraviolet immersion lithography (DUV) machines and etching and deposition equipment to unrestricted wafer fabs in China, and provide on-site maintenance and spare parts support. This created a window of opportunity for China to expand its production capacity for advanced logic chips and high-bandwidth memory. The MATCH Act requires the executive branch to urge the Netherlands, Japan, and other allies to fully align their export restrictions on semiconductor manufacturing equipment with US standards, bridging the regulatory gaps in equipment categories and after-sales service. The Dutch government has held multiple rounds of communication with the US on this issue, striving to reduce the impact of US extraterritorial jurisdiction on the normal operations of its equipment companies while cooperating with multilateral security coordination. The four acts complement each other, forming a complete institutional framework covering manufacturing equipment, physical chips, cloud access, and administrative approvals.

Chapter 4 The Impact of Upgraded Computing Power Regulation on China's Artificial Intelligence Industry

4.1 The Contraction of Offshore Computing Power Changes the Cost Structure of Large Model Training

With Nvidia's internal compliance restructuring and the accelerated legislative process in the US Congress, Chinese artificial intelligence companies are first facing a substantial narrowing of overseas computing power leasing channels. Before the formal legislation is implemented, in order to reduce its own regulatory risks, Nvidia has proactively reduced more than half of its pre-approved buyer list in Asia in recent months, and guided its global cloud partners to increase the proportion of services from non-Chinese customers to more than 51%, while requiring some cloud vendors to cooperate in verifying the identity of the final computing power user. Following Jensen Huang's departure, emerging cloud computing operators in Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and Europe and the United States are bound to accelerate the cleanup of high-risk businesses involving China, driven by concerns about hardware supply and debt financing security. The past practice of some domestic R&D institutions acquiring the latest generation of accelerator card clusters through overseas distributed data centers will face higher compliance review thresholds and uncertainty regarding supply disruptions. Especially after the new BIS remote computing power regulations were issued on November 16th, the arrival of equipment in the data center, the signing of contracts, and the prepayment of rent no longer guarantee continued service. Existing services must obtain a license within 90 days, and the licensing conditions for renting US-owned overseas data centers or sharing computing power with recommended businesses must also be reviewed. Domestic companies heavily reliant on single overseas clusters for training have recently had to prioritize the refund of unused fees, the export and migration of training data and model checkpoints. The tightening of hardware acquisition channels directly alters the cost function and technology selection preferences for large-scale model development in China. When simply increasing the number of chips using the latest process technology to increase model size becomes uneconomical or even infeasible, the focus of engineering optimization naturally shifts to improving the efficiency of word generation per unit of computing power. At the model architecture level, controlling the proportion of single activation parameters in hybrid expert models (MoE), compressing key-value caches (KV Cache) in long context scenarios, and improving sparse attention mechanisms have become the main means of offsetting hardware memory bandwidth constraints. At the commercial application level, enterprises no longer blindly pursue repetitive training on all-around ultra-large parameter bases, but instead pay more attention to the inference cost-effectiveness of medium-sized models in vertical industry scenarios. While computing power constraints increase the difficulty of cutting-edge exploration, they also prompt industry funds and computing power resources to concentrate more quickly on R&D teams with underlying systems engineering capabilities.

4.2 Tightening External Channels Accelerates Commercialization Verification of Domestic Computing Power

From the perspective of the incentive mechanism for industrial evolution, the US's comprehensive blockade of offshore computing power leasing and reduction of chip supply has objectively produced another profound impact: it has eliminated the wait-and-see mentality of Chinese artificial intelligence companies towards external computing power channels, and accelerated the commercialization integration of domestic computing power chips and local software stacks. In the semiconductor industry, whether an accelerator card can move from "usable" to "easy to use" depends on whether enough front-line algorithm teams continuously use it in real large-scale training and high-concurrency inference tasks, and continuously improve the compiler, communication library, and underlying operators in practice. In the past few years, as long as companies could still access NVIDIA computing power through compliant hardware reduction or leasing from overseas data centers, most teams preferred to use the mature CUDA environment for short-term business reasons, such as saving code migration and debugging time. This made it difficult for domestically produced chips to enter the most critical pre-training stage of cutting-edge models. As external alternative channels gradually close, the long-term certainty of migrating to domestic computing power architectures has begun to outweigh the short-term engineering modification costs, leading to a significant increase in the depth of collaboration between leading domestic model vendors and domestic chip companies. Since 2026, this shift has been validated on several benchmark models: In February, Zhipu's flagship model GLM-5 was trained entirely on a Huawei Ascend 910B cluster with a scale of 100,000 cards and the Ascend framework, and achieved inference support for multiple domestic accelerator cards; between April and August, DeepSeek launched the V4 hybrid expert model with 1.6 trillion total parameters, and simultaneously open-sourced inference operators and community plugins deeply optimized for Ascend processors; in June, Meituan's LongCat 2.0 model also completed the pre-training process from scratch based on domestic computing power clusters. As leading commercial applications and basic models continue to run on domestic hardware, the shortcomings in the software ecosystem can be gradually made up through high-frequency engineering feedback, and the funds that originally flowed to the overseas computing power leasing market will also flow back to support the iteration of domestic wafer manufacturing, advanced packaging, and cluster interconnection technologies. 4.3 Hardware Infrastructure Differentiation Weakens Cross-Border Open Source Software Collaboration Another structural spillover effect brought about by the upgrading of computing power controls is the dismantling of the symbiotic relationship between the Chinese and American engineering communities in the field of artificial intelligence open source software. Over the past two years, a noteworthy phenomenon has emerged in the global open source large model ecosystem: Chinese research teams, constrained by hardware performance and quantity, have developed and open-sourced a number of high-quality underlying communication and matrix operation libraries to fully exploit the computing efficiency of existing NVIDIA chips. These include DeepEP and DeepGEMM for hybrid expert architectures, as well as the attention-optimized kernel FlashKDA released by Dark Side of the Moon. These underlying software innovations have been widely integrated into mainstream international open source inference frameworks such as vLLM and SGLang, significantly reducing the computing power costs for small and medium-sized technology companies and startups worldwide to deploy large models. For NVIDIA, a thriving open source model ecosystem was originally a crucial support for maintaining its market position. As North American hyperscale cloud service providers such as Google, Amazon, and Microsoft deploy their own proprietary chips on a large scale, the long-term bargaining power of closed-source giants over general-purpose graphics processors continues to strengthen. Only if the open-source model maintains strong competitiveness will enterprises worldwide continue to procure NVIDIA hardware for private deployments and regional cloud service providers. During his tenure, Jensen Huang actively supported the open-source community, and NVIDIA's engineering team maintained close technical collaboration with Chinese open-source labs. Following Huang's departure and the implementation of remote access restrictions, NVIDIA, now managed by professional managers, is expected to reduce its open-source technology collaboration with China due to compliance considerations and short-term financial returns. Simultaneously, as the Chinese R&D team shifts its optimization focus to domestically developed heterogeneous chip architectures, its underlying operators and compilation tools will no longer be directly compatible with US hardware, and some key performance optimizations may even become proprietary internal technologies. The slowdown in the flow of cross-border open-source technology will objectively increase the difficulty for Western startups to obtain low-cost open-source inference solutions.

Chapter 5: Long-Term Evolution Trends of Global Computing Infrastructure

5.1 The Dominance of a Single Hardware Architecture Gradually Loosens

From a long-term perspective of the evolution of the global technology industry, Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO of Nvidia marks the end of a phase where global computing power expansion was dominated by a single company, a single founder, and a single software and hardware ecosystem. Over the past decade, global artificial intelligence computing has been built on a highly integrated transnational division of labor: relying on Taiwan's advanced wafer foundry, South Korea's high-bandwidth memory chips, Nvidia's parallel computing architecture and CUDA software system, combined with the vast engineering talent pool of China and the United States, the entire industry has been able to rapidly iterate along unified technical standards. Jensen Huang, with his strategic vision and business acumen as a founder, managed to maintain the operation of this transnational business network amidst a complex geopolitical environment. His departure indicates that corporate-level business maneuvering can no longer offset the institutional fragmentation brought about by great power security competition. In the upcoming industry cycle, the global computing power market will simultaneously experience horizontal competition diffusion and vertical regional differentiation. Within the Western market, Nvidia, now under professional management, will place greater emphasis on capital expenditure discipline and shareholder returns. The past practice of relying on the founder's personal promises to massively lock up upstream storage and foundry capacity will be somewhat curbed. It is expected that by around 2028, a larger proportion of advanced manufacturing and storage capacity will flow to cloud giants' self-developed dedicated chips and competitors such as Broadcom and AMD. At the transnational level, if the US Congress passes legislation to block remote cloud access and mandate chip location verification, the gray area connecting East and West's computing power supply and demand will disappear. The global computing power infrastructure is more likely to evolve into a binary structure where the US ecosystem and domestic independent ecosystems evolve independently. 5.2 Systems Engineering Capabilities Become the Core Measure of Computing Power Competition While the comprehensive upgrade of export control legislation will undoubtedly pose a continued obstacle to China's acquisition of cutting-edge semiconductor equipment and computing hardware manufacturing in the coming years, the long-term competitiveness of computing infrastructure is not solely determined by the process node of a single chip. As artificial intelligence applications gradually expand from early large-scale pre-training to high-frequency complex inference and industrial-level deployment, the benchmark for measuring the performance of computing power systems is shifting from single-card peak floating-point computing power to comprehensive system capabilities encompassing high-speed cluster interconnection, power supply, algorithm architecture efficiency, and industry scenario implementation. Under the condition that the manufacturing process of a single chip is limited by external equipment, system-level engineering innovation provides a clear path to breakthrough. By leveraging high-bandwidth optical interconnects and supernode technology to network and coordinate large-scale domestically produced accelerator cards, and utilizing China's cost advantages in power generation capacity, grid dispatching, and data center infrastructure construction to distribute cluster energy consumption, combined with continuous reduction of computational and communication redundancy at the algorithm level, it is entirely possible to compensate for the gap in physical performance of a single card in terms of overall cluster throughput and cost per word inference. The resignation of Jensen Huang triggered a tightening of US control over computing power in China, closing off convenient external computing channels while also prompting China's AI industry to concentrate resources more on underlying hardware manufacturing, system software compilation, and high-value industry applications. In this new stage of parallel evolution of two technological systems, the true determinant of the long-term industrial landscape will be which side can more sustainably translate computing power into productivity gains for the real economy through energy and capital investment.

data.title: Why is it said that the "next stablecoin moment" is tokenized stocks?
data.description:
Author: Token Terminal, stablecoin, tokenized asset, and on-chain financial data platform; Translator: Gu Yu, ChainCatcher

In March 2020, the market capitalization of stablecoins surpassed $4.8 billion. Since then, the market capitalization of stablecoins has increased 59 times, reaching $285 billion. With the passage of the GENIUS Act, a federal stablecoin law, in July 2025, the United States now regulates and supports stablecoins as a way to expand the influence of the US dollar. On November 13, 2026, the market capitalization of tokenized stocks reached the same $4.8 billion.

Tokenized stocks are blockchain tokens that track shares of publicly traded companies. Most tokenized stocks are backed 1:1 by shares held by custodians, who are regulated institutions responsible for safeguarding the shares. These tokens trade 24/7 and can be used in on-chain applications.

The market is growing rapidly.

Over the past 12 months, the market capitalization of tokenized stocks has increased 9.1 times, and the number of holders has increased 40 times, reaching 5.9 million.

https://tokenterminal.com/explorer/tokenized-assets/stocks

Tokenized stocks are following the path of stablecoins reaching a market capitalization of $285 billion, and the reasons for supporting tokenized stocks in the US are the same as those for supporting stablecoins.

1. An Emerging Stablecoin-Level Category

Token stablecoins, designed to maintain a value of $1, are the clearest precedent. Every crisis since 2020, from the COVID crash to the Terra and FTX crashes and the SVB collapse, has tested whether holders trust stablecoins, and the market capitalization of stablecoins has recovered after each crisis.

These crises have also shown which designs can withstand the test. Terra, which relies on algorithms rather than reserves...

UST crashed, while the two major stablecoins, USDT and USDC, primarily backed by cash and US Treasury bonds, currently account for 86% of the stablecoin market capitalization. Most tokenized stocks use the same reserve-backed design. https://tokenterminal.com/explorer/tokenized-assets/stablecoins The market capitalization of tokenized stocks is now comparable to that of stablecoins in March 2020, and tokenized stocks reached this level much faster. From the moment their respective market capitalizations surpassed $1 billion, tokenized stocks took 8 months to reach $4.8 billion, while stablecoins took 11 months. Tokenized stocks are also emerging in a more mature market, with wallets, exchanges, and DeFi venues already in place, and the regulatory environment is clearer than that of stablecoins in 2020, including an SEC exemption for tokenized stock trading starting in September 2026. src="https://img.jinse.com.cn/7523606_watermarknone.png" alt="Why is the 'next stablecoin moment' said to be tokenized stocks?" " preview="3" data-pswp-uid="3">

https://tokenterminal.com/docs/mcp/introduction

The demand served by tokenized stocks is enormous. Foreign investors hold $25.2 trillion in US stocks, which has grown by 23% in the past 12 months, while the market capitalization of tokenized stocks is only equivalent to 0.02% of foreign holdings. If 1% of foreign-held US stocks were moved on-chain, the scale would reach $252 billion, approximately 50 times the current tokenized stock market.

https://tokenterminal.com/docs/mcp/introduction

2. The US has the same interests in tokenized stocks as it does in stablecoins

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has stated that stablecoins could become one of the largest buyers of US Treasury bonds and help expand the dollar's influence overseas. Tokenized stocks can play the same role as US stocks, and four characteristics of the tokenized stock market demonstrate this parallel: the assets are US, the buyers are foreign, the tokens are backed by real shares, and the majority of the shares are held by US custodians.

Most tokenized stocks track US-listed assets. US-listed stocks and exchange-traded funds (ETFs) account for 88% of the market capitalization of tokenized stocks.

https://tokenterminal.com/explorer/fact-sheets?view=map

Almost all tokenized stocks are backed by real shares. Tokens backed by underlying shares at a 1:1 ratio account for 91% of the market capitalization of tokenized stocks, which is the same structure as stablecoins backed by the US dollar. Therefore, one token sold overseas corresponds to one share purchased in the US market.

https://tokenterminal.com/explorer/tokenized-assets/stocks?stocksReferenceAssets=mstr,strc

3. On-chain use makes tokenized stocks harder to replace

Every new use case for stablecoins, whether in exchanges, lending markets, or payments, makes them more useful to others and harder to replace. Tokenized stocks are beginning to follow the same use case. DeFi TVL, the value of tokenized stocks deposited into on-chain applications such as lending markets and trading pools, has grown 24 times in the past year, reaching $300 million. Currently, deposits represent 6.3% of the market capitalization of tokenized stocks, up from 2.4% a year ago, and each deposit adds liquidity for the next trader and earns yield for the holder.

https://tokenterminal.com/explorer/tokenized-assets/stocks?stocksMetric=asset_tvl

Weekend trading provides holders with another reason to stay on-chain, as US exchanges are closed on Saturdays and Sundays. In October 2026, weekends accounted for 18% of tokenized stock trading volume on decentralized exchanges (DEXs), or $2.4 billion, 83 times the level of a year ago. Holders can act based on the news before the market opens on Monday.

https://tokenterminal.com/explorer/tokenized-assets/stocks?stocksMetric=asset_trading_volume

4. Restrictions on asset-backed tokens will drive demand to perpetual futures marketplaces

A key risk of tokenized stocks comes from regulation. If US regulators restrict tokenized stocks backed 1:1 by shares, demand for US stocks in non-US markets is likely to shift to perpetual futures (perps), which are price-tracking contracts with no expiration date and no underlying stock.

The stock perpetual futures market is already growing. Trade.xyz is a perpetual futures exchange built on Hyperliquid.

The perpetual futures market is already growing.

It's a blockchain designed for trading, and the exchange has launched US stock and index contracts. The open interest in Trade.xyz's stock perpetual contracts—the value of open positions—has grown 55 times in the past year, reaching $1.54 billion. Each position in a perpetual contract doesn't require an underlying stock, so less of the demand moving to perpetual contracts ultimately ends up in US stocks and US custodians, and perpetual contracts don't pay dividends that are taxable in the US. Supporting asset-backed tokens allows more overseas demand to remain in US stocks. " preview="13" data-pswp-uid="13">

https://tokenterminal.com/explorer/projects/tradexyz/xyzspcx?metric1=open-interest

Core Conclusions

Today's tokenized stocks look like stablecoins in 2020. Tokenized stocks use the same reserve-backed design, grew their market capitalization from $1 billion to $4.8 billion much faster, and relied on $25.2 trillion in overseas holdings of US stocks. This gives the US the same reason to support tokenized stocks as it does to support stablecoins, because restricting asset-backed tokens would push the same overseas demand toward perpetual contracts, where less demand would reach US stocks.

data.title: How to protect your wealth during geopolitical storms?
data.description:
Author: Christina Comben; Translator: Chopper, Foresight News

Geopolitical conflicts, cyberattacks, and power grid failures could strike at any time, and more and more governments are beginning to remind their citizens to prepare for major disasters.

In the UK, people are responding to the government's "Be Ready" campaign by stockpiling canned food and bottled water.

Fighter jets flying over the Middle East, rumors of a dirty bomb attack on Washington, D.C., and the world's largest software company experiencing a full-day outage—the possibility of disaster hitting our doorstep is becoming increasingly real.

But what about your money then? How can you protect your wealth while ensuring access to it in case of system failure?

The key lies in two things: choosing assets that will retain their value even if the world is engulfed in flames, and having access to funds in an emergency.

Regarding the first point, Maximilian Kunkel, Chief Investment Officer for Ultra-High Net Worth Clients at UBS, one of the world's largest wealth management firms, told Magazine, "We want to remind you not to assume that any single asset is safe in all circumstances." He said wealthy investors should focus on building a portfolio that is "resilient across multiple scenarios," has sufficient liquidity, and is well-diversified across asset classes, currencies, and geographies. The Boundaries Between Bitcoin, Gold, and "Safe-Haven Assets" UBS's 2026 Global Family Office Report covers families with an average net worth of $2.7 billion, of which 64% listed major geopolitical conflicts as their biggest concern for the next 12 months. However, these investors have not flocked to the cryptocurrency market in an attempt to preserve their wealth. "24% of family offices report exposure to cryptocurrencies or digital assets, but within those investments, the allocation is typically only around 1%," explains Hadley Stern, head of institutional business at Silence Laboratories and founder of Fidelity Digital Assets. He adds that financial institutions may now classify Bitcoin and gold in the same category, but Bitcoin hasn't yet gained the same safe-haven reputation. "Gold has been around for thousands of years… Bitcoin is less than twenty. But the logic is the same: a scarce asset that isn't a liability to any other party," he says. He advised against using it as a reliable hedge during a crisis: "I'm a bit cautious about the term 'hedge,'" he said. "Bitcoin remains highly volatile and often trades alongside other risky assets during market sell-offs." In contrast, cash is useful in emergencies but not suitable for "long-term preservation of value," he said. Michael D'Alessio, COO of digital asset trading platform Talos, told Magazine that there are early signs that Bitcoin is beginning to resemble gold more. He said that during the period of volatility surrounding the US midterm elections, Bitcoin's correlation with stocks remained high; however, its correlation with gold also increased significantly during the same period, reaching approximately 0.75 over a 30-day period as of early August. "This is a significant shift, and it's exactly the kind of signal institutional investors are now looking for." [Image: 30-day rolling daily yield correlation between Bitcoin and gold. Source: Talos / Coin Metrics] The risk isn't just losing money, it's not being able to withdraw it. The collapse of Mt. Gox, and more recently, the collapse of a Paraguayan bank, demonstrates that "the safety of an asset depends on the system that holds it," Stern said. Instead of automatically turning to Bitcoin or gold when tensions escalate, the risk committees within these institutions are starting to ask other questions: "Where are the assets? In which jurisdiction? Who can freeze them? What if counterparties or payment channels are shut down for a week?" he said. "These used to be back-office questions, but now they're being discussed at the board level." Kunkel said concerns about major geopolitical conflicts are prompting wealthy families to consider "not just asset allocation, but also where to put assets, currency exposure, liquidity, and jurisdictional diversification." A UBS report found that 88% of family offices hold depository assets in two or more jurisdictions, and 30% are increasing or considering increasing currency diversification. The institutional version of "filling storage rooms" is a good thing. Fortunately, banks and custodians are also making actual disaster preparedness plans. "Regulators expect institutions to plan for 'serious but reasonable' events," Stern explained, such as cloud service outages, cyberattacks, the collapse of key suppliers, or market closures for several days, and to "prove they can maintain the most critical services in these situations." The UK government advises the public to stockpile supplies. Source: Gov.uk

For custodians, this means testing: if a signing location goes offline, can assets still be transferred? If a data center is gone, how quickly can operations recover? Stern says that while families might fill their storage rooms to prepare for emergencies, the institutional approach is: not relying on any single thing—not relying on a single custodian, a single key holder, a single cloud service, or a single bank.

Similarly, investors need to figure out which assets can be withdrawn quickly and which cannot, and "maintain enough liquidity to weather a bad period without being forced to sell."

Kunkel says that capital preservation "does not mean eliminating volatility, but maintaining enough liquidity and diversification to withstand volatility," avoiding becoming a forced seller.

When something truly serious happens, diversification can protect a portfolio from market shocks, but if the infrastructure supporting it fails, you may not be able to access your funds.

Hedging is not just about owning the right things; it's about having access to them even when the system crashes.

data.title: Anthropic's stock price nearly fell below its IPO price on its second day of trading: The underwriting syndicate is under pressure.
data.description:
Author: Gao Zhimou, Wall Street Insights

Anthropic announced Friday morning that the "greenshoe" option (over-allotment option) for its IPO had been exercised. With this option exercised, subsequent market support measures have decreased. Furthermore, approximately 300 million Anthropic shares will become tradable on December 15th, potentially leading to further selling pressure.

The largest IPO in history experienced a sharp sell-off on its second day of trading.

Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic (ANT) plunged as much as 15% intraday on Friday, reaching a low of just 5 cents above its IPO price, before closing down 8.5% at $88.91, wiping out approximately $109 billion in market capitalization in a single day.

... This violent market shakeup dashed market expectations that Anthropic could reverse the AI ​​sector's downward trend. On Friday, core AI stocks such as Nvidia, Meta, and Oracle fell in tandem with Anthropic, wiping out $4 trillion in Nasdaq market capitalization. The market turmoil also affected Anthropic's main competitor, OpenAI, which is pushing forward with a new round of massive funding valuing the company at $1.25 trillion and is eager to go public next year. However, sources close to Anthropic and its lead underwriters insist that the IPO was still a success, emphasizing that the company raised over $100 billion through the IPO and concurrent share offering, and held above the offering price even during one of the most intense market sell-offs in history, with Friday's closing price still 7% higher than the offering price.

The allocation favored existing shareholders, with 60% of participating institutions leaving empty-handed

Anthropic showed signs of weakness on its first day of trading.

Before noon on Thursday, the stock opened at more than 30% above its offering price, but buying enthusiasm quickly waned, and it trended lower throughout the day, ultimately closing up 17%.

Some investors questioned the company's and investment banks' allocation arrangements for the $81 billion IPO shares. According to sources, more than half of the IPO shares went to existing investors who already held company equity, including Altimeter Capital, Lightspeed Venture Partners, and Menlo Ventures.

This unusually high proportion reflects Anthropic executives' willingness to reward early backers. Some of these early backers are venture capital firms whose existing holdings are subject to lock-up periods. According to industry practice, venture capital firms typically do not receive large allocations of new shares in an IPO, as these shares can be immediately sold on the secondary market to lock in profits. Furthermore, sources familiar with the matter stated that Anthropic also allocated a significant proportion of its IPO shares to large investment institutions such as Citadel, leading some unsuccessful investors to speculate that the company prioritized major clients of its Claude model. Normally, listed companies and investment banking advisors carefully screen subscription requests, spending several days selecting the best shareholder list to ensure stable post-IPO share price performance and a stable shareholding structure. However, according to some sources, approximately 60% of the institutions that applied to subscribe at the IPO price received nothing, including a large number of hedge funds and large mutual funds. Many other institutions received only partial allocations—according to the Wall Street Journal, asset management giant BlackRock submitted subscription applications for approximately $10 billion, but ultimately only received about half. The opening price was questioned, and immediate employee cashing out exacerbated selling pressure. Besides the allocation controversy, Wall Street is also scrutinizing the offering price and lock-up arrangements. One hedge fund manager questioned whether the investment banks that helped determine the opening timing and price may have set the opening price too high, creating an irreversible downward momentum. However, delaying the opening also carries risks, as the share price could continue to rise during this period. Meanwhile, Anthropic's IPO included a rare clause allowing some current and former employees to immediately sell approximately 300 million shares, worth about $26 billion at the IPO price. In a typical IPO, employee stock ownership plans usually face a lock-up period of several months. This reduction in shareholding likely increased downward pressure on the stock price. Unlike Wall Street's anxiety, several AI practitioners in San Francisco said they largely ignored the pullback in Anthropic's stock price. They were more focused on another piece of news on Friday—an Anthropic mathematician claimed that Claude had solved the "Millennium Prize Problem," a puzzle that had baffled humanity for 167 years. Many see this as a sign that AI is surpassing human intelligence. Furthermore, these employees stated that even at the current stock price, many Anthropic employees' shares are still worth millions of dollars more than at the beginning of the week. AI Deals in Turmoil, Greenshoe Option Exercised Anthropic and its advisors knew that proceeding with an IPO during the most turbulent AI deal to date was extremely risky, but they never expected to encounter this "perfect storm." Rising borrowing costs for cloud computing companies and the lingering effects of the Nvidia controversy have exacerbated market anxiety in recent weeks. Investors had hoped that Anthropic, a pure AI giant, could turn the tide and revive the market, but this did not happen. From the perspective of the underwriting investment banks, as long as Anthropic's share price did not fall below the IPO price, the listing was still considered a success. However, once the share price fell below the IPO price, a key tool that investment banks could use to stabilize the price became ineffective. Anthropic announced on Friday morning that the "greenshoe" option (over-allotment option) for this IPO had been exercised. The "greenshoe" option allows underwriters to offer investors an additional 15% of the shares issued. Underwriters can then either buy back these shares from the company at the IPO price or repurchase them from the open market to support the share price if it falls below the IPO price. With the option being exercised early, subsequent market support measures have decreased. Furthermore, approximately 300 million Anthropic shares will become tradable on December 15th, potentially leading to further selling pressure.

data.title: A generational buying opportunity for BTC is approaching; the AI ​​crisis may have triggered the final bottom.
data.description:
Author: 100y, Head of Research, Four Pillars; Translator: Gu Yu, ChainCatcher

I woke up late on Saturday morning, made myself pasta and salmon, and then sat down at my computer. I couldn't believe my eyes. BTC was trading at $55,000.

Is the crypto market officially dead? Or is this a generational buying opportunity?

... Here are my thoughts: We are very close to a bottoming-out buying opportunity for BTC. Assuming BTC eventually enters another bull market, the $45,000 to $55,000 range looks like an attractive entry point. There is still a significant possibility that we haven't seen the bottom of this cycle yet. Technical and on-chain indicators such as moving averages and MVRV suggest there may be more downside potential. Given what's happening in the AI ​​industry, macroeconomic factors could also push BTC prices lower. My baseline scenario is that a crisis in the AI ​​industry will trigger the final bottom for BTC sometime within the next year, followed by a trend reversal driven by US credit expansion and monetary easing. Let me briefly explain why I think this is the most likely scenario. 1. The Crypto Industry is Stronger Than Ever Before Before diving into technical analysis, market cycles, and on-chain data, let's take a step back and look at the broader crypto industry, to which BTC belongs. As I'll discuss later, I'm seeing a growing number of posts on X claiming that crypto has accomplished nothing compared to AI and that the entire industry is essentially useless. I completely disagree. The image above is from Four Pillars' upcoming year-end report. My current assessment of the crypto industry is that several sectors have clearly found their PMF (Power, Faith, and Momentum). The problem, however, is that adoption is extremely concentrated in a few areas. First, there's the more speculative aspect of crypto, including memecoins, perpetual futures, and prediction markets. These sectors consistently attract stable user activity regardless of the broader crypto market conditions. Perpetual contracts and prediction markets, in particular, represent entirely new ways of trading financial markets, with enormous growth potential. There's a reason why Robinhood, Coinbase, and various traditional financial institutions are so focused on these markets. Second, there's the rise of crypto as the next generation of financial infrastructure, primarily through stablecoins and RWAs. Traditional financial infrastructure is extremely fragmented. Different asset classes and use cases rely on completely independent backend systems. Blockchain is increasingly seen as one of the few technologies capable of integrating these fragmented systems. Just look at DTCC's tokenization initiatives, ICE and NYSE's tokenized stock trading plans, and the stablecoin initiatives being explored by large banks like Bank of America. There's a reason why so many financial institutions, large and small, are investing resources in stablecoins, RWAs, and blockchain infrastructure. While BTC may currently be trading at $55,000 to $56,000, the crypto industry is arguably finding more genuine PMF (Profitability, Fundamentals, and Sense Time) than ever before and is increasingly integrating into the existing financial system. Regardless of market prices or sentiment, the crypto industry is vibrant. If you consider the future of financial infrastructure, it's hard to imagine this industry not growing significantly from here. 2. The 300-week moving average (WMA) has been breached. [Image of BTC buying opportunity and AI crisis as potential bottom] There's an old saying in the crypto world: "The 200-week moving average is the bottom." In major market crashes, including the 2018 bear market, the COVID-19 crash, the Terra crash, and the FTX bankruptcy, the 200-week moving average has always been an extremely useful psychological reference point for identifying BTC bottoms. But this time, the situation is different. The recent sell-off has broken below both the 200-week moving average (WMA) and the 300-week moving average (WMA). BTC is currently approaching the 350-week moving average (WMA), a level that has historically acted as a near-perfect floor. If BTC touches the 350-week moving average in the short term, the corresponding price would be approximately $52,000. Regardless, BTC has broken below the 200-week moving average (WMA), one of its strongest psychological support levels in history. This fact suggests that, assuming another bull market eventually arrives, we may be very close to the bottom. We've seen similar situations before. In June 2022, after the Terra crash and subsequent collapses of Celsius and 3AC, BTC briefly traded about 20% below its 200-week moving average (WMA). It took BTC approximately nine months to regain its 200-week moving average (200WMA), and another 14 months to clearly break away from that level and begin its next major upward move. Currently, BTC is trading about 18% below its 200WMA, putting us in a very similar position. If history repeats itself, we could certainly see another dip. However, we might also be entering a period where BTC trades sideways for the next year before the next major breakout, gradually rising along its 200WMA.

3. The Beginning of a New Four-Year Cycle

I believe one of the least convincing yet most powerful narratives is the four-year cycle theory of Bitcoin. I don't think there are any fundamental reasons enough to believe it will work so consistently.

However, the time intervals between the bottoms and tops are so strikingly similar that it sometimes almost feels like the Illuminati is secretly controlling the price of BTC.

Since its 2015 bottom, BTC has repeatedly experienced rallies of approximately 1,061 to 1,068 days, followed by declines of approximately 363 days. Combined with Bitcoin's halving cycle, this pattern has become an extremely powerful narrative shaping investor psychology. This is especially important for assets like BTC that don't generate cash flow and are heavily influenced by macroeconomic conditions and market sentiment. For these assets, the narrative is crucial. If this historical pattern continues, we should now be nearing the end of a bear market and about to embark on a new bullish phase. However, there is a significant risk. More than 363 days have passed since the last high, and BTC's decline has exceeded historical timeframes. I don't believe this alone is enough to declare the four-year cycle invalid. But if BTC continues to deviate from this pattern, we need to seriously reassess whether this theory still holds true. 4. MVRV is approaching a break below 1. [Image of BTC at a new generation buying opportunity; AI crisis may create the final bottom] MVRV stands for Market Value to Realized Value. It is calculated by dividing the current market capitalization of BTC by its realized market capitalization; realized market capitalization is valued based on the price at which each BTC last moved on-chain. In short, a lower MVRV means that BTC's current market capitalization is relatively low relative to the total cost base estimated by investors. Historically, periods when MVRV falls below 1 have often presented attractive long-term buying opportunities. In previous cycles, BTC typically reached its final bottom about 1 to 6 months after MVRV fell below 1. Subsequently, it often consolidated near the MVRV-below-1 range for about 6 to 12 months before resuming its upward trend. MVRV hasn't fallen below 1 yet, but we're very close. This makes me increasingly optimistic that a strong long-term buying opportunity may be approaching. Here's another encouraging detail: the MVRV bottom of each cycle has been gradually rising. Since 2011, historical MVRV lows have followed a pattern of approximately 0.395 → 0.564 → 0.691 → 0.760. If this trend continues, there's a considerable chance the current cycle's MVRV bottom won't be as deep as earlier cycles. Assuming realized market capitalization remains constant and the next MVRV bottom follows historical trends, landing around 0.8, we can estimate the BTC bottom to be around $43,000. 5. BTC is approaching its mining cost trade. Source: CryptoQuant. CryptoQuant estimates the cost of mining 1 BTC by analyzing the financial disclosures of Marathon Holdings, one of the major publicly traded Bitcoin mining companies. As of Q3 2026, the cost was approximately $62,900 per BTC. Historically, Bitcoin miners' production costs have been a useful signal for identifying potential market bottoms. When the price of BTC trades below its production cost, miners have less incentive to sell newly mined tokens at a loss. Of course, this has changed. Halvings have reduced BTC production, and many Bitcoin mining companies are now diversifying into AI data center businesses. Therefore, I wouldn't consider mining costs as the absolute bottom for BTC prices. However, I think it's still a useful indicator to keep in mind when assessing where the market bottom might be. 6. BTC Has Decoupled from M2 Liquidity Many investors view BTC as digital gold with a fixed supply. Within this framework, the price of BTC, denominated in US dollars, should typically benefit when liquidity expands in the financial system. Historically, we have also seen BTC surge during periods of expansion in the US M2 money supply. However, an interesting phenomenon has recently emerged. Throughout 2026, US M2 liquidity expanded again, yet BTC continued to fall sharply. The correlation between BTC price and M2 liquidity has dropped to near zero. In my view, this suggests that BTC may be significantly undervalued relative to the current level of liquidity available in the financial system. 7. Market Sentiment is Extremely Poor. [Image of a BTC buy signal and potential AI crisis as the final bottom is shown.] Thanks to Jeff Dorman, iruletrenches, Beanie, and Austin Campbell for their posts. Historically, extreme bearish sentiment has been a useful signal that the market is nearing its bottom. Right now, crypto sentiment is almost at its worst. Over the past few weeks, X has been flooded with posts claiming that crypto is a waste of time, the entire industry is meaningless, and virtually every crypto token is garbage. What's even more interesting is the amount of attention and endorsement these posts have garnered from investors. Google Trends tells a similar story. Search interest in Bitcoin has fallen back to levels last seen around 2020, near its lowest point since then. Historically, moments when everyone abandons crypto have often turned out to be some of the best buying opportunities. 8. Monetary Expansion Is Inevitable When considering market liquidity over the next three years, one thing I'm particularly confident about is that AI will ultimately lead to a massive expansion of dollar liquidity. This largely aligns with the argument presented by Arthur Hayes in his article *Situationship*. The logic is simple. If the AI ​​bubble doesn't burst and the industry continues to grow, private credit creation, including bank lending, will continue to expand. If the AI ​​bubble bursts, the US government will inevitably respond with credit expansion and monetary easing, just as it did during the 2008 financial crisis. Recent developments increasingly favor the second scenario. Following a series of controversies surrounding Jensen Huang and his resignation as CEO of NVIDIA, coupled with the Democratic Party's landslide victory in the midterm elections and the resulting pressure on the construction and development of AI data centers, investors have begun to question the financing structure supporting the AI ​​industry. Whether these developments will ultimately trigger a significant correction in the AI ​​bubble remains to be seen. However, if the AI ​​bubble does burst, I find it hard to imagine the US government standing idly by and doing nothing. AI is no longer just another industry driven by market supply and demand. It is becoming a strategic national asset. In a world where it is increasingly believed that whichever country achieves AGI or ASI first will likely dominate the next era of global power, the US cannot afford to fall behind China. In this context, I believe the US has virtually no choice but to support the AI ​​industry through aggressive credit creation and monetary expansion.

Recall the 2008 financial crisis and the 2020 COVID crash. The time between the announcement of quantitative easing and the market bottoming out has shortened significantly. My interpretation is that investors have learned how the market reacts to monetary easing and are increasingly pricing it in. If the AI ​​bubble bursts and the government announces aggressive credit and monetary expansion again, I expect BTC to potentially rebound strongly.

... 9. Worst-Case Scenario So far, I've explained why I believe the next 6 to 12 months could offer an attractive entry point for BTC, assuming we eventually enter the next bull market. But let's look at the argument from the opposite perspective. Almost every point I've made so far can also be interpreted as a bearish signal. A healthy crypto industry doesn't necessarily mean higher BTC prices. Even if stablecoins, RWA, and blockchain technology replace a large portion of the global financial back-end infrastructure in the next five to ten years, there's no guarantee that BTC will capture that value. A breach of the 200-week moving average (200WMA) and 300-week moving average (300WMA) could mean that BTC has lost momentum. Price levels that previously served as reliable bottoms may no longer be relevant. The four-year cycle may have been broken. Historically, a bear market should last about 363 days. We are currently on the 411th day of the decline. A MVRV below 1 and BTC trading below miners' production costs do not guarantee that the bottom has been reached. Especially now that many Bitcoin mining companies are also operating AI data centers, this could be changing historical dynamics. Despite expanding M2 liquidity, BTC is still falling, which could be a structural warning sign. Funds that might have previously flowed into BTC may now be being absorbed by the AI ​​industry. And that's not all. Potential capitulation selling by DAT companies, the threat posed by quantum computing, and continued selling pressure from stolen funds related to events involving Binance and other platforms could all pose significant risks to BTC's future performance. BTC may not recover as historical cycles suggest, for many reasons. 10. Buy BTC, and thank me later. Ultimately, buying BTC is betting on its future price to be even higher. To have faith in this bet, you need to answer a fundamental question: Where does Bitcoin's value come from? Some see BTC as the asset that best represents the growth and scale of the broader digital asset industry. Others see it as digital gold, a hedge against long-term fiat currency devaluation. Still others value it as a decentralized currency, freely held and transferred by anyone in the world without dependence on governments or centralized institutions. Personally, one of my biggest reasons for being bullish on BTC in the long term, ironically, is the advancement of AI. AI will dramatically increase the supply of things we once considered scarce. Software, content, knowledge work, and countless other things that have historically required human time and labor will become increasingly cheaper and more abundant. I believe that in a world where almost everything becomes abundant, things that cannot be artificially created or inflated, and systems that do not require trust in centralized authorities, will become relatively more valuable. This is why I believe the technological value of blockchain, especially its decentralization and verifiability, will become even more important in the AI ​​era. And BTC is the asset that has best exemplified these principles for the longest time. It does not depend on the profits of any single company, nor on the policies of any single government. No single entity can unilaterally increase its supply, and participants around the world can independently verify and enforce the same set of rules. I believe the next six to twelve months will be a crucial period to test this belief, and may also offer one of the most interesting opportunities to bet on it. Buy BTC, and thank me later.

data.title: Lean: I believe Anthropic's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct.
data.description:
Author: Gao Zhimou, Wall Street Insights

Traditional mathematical breakthroughs rely on peer review of papers, judging the validity of each step of reasoning. However, faced with over 250,000 pages of proof drafts that no one can read in the short term, the formal verification software Lean has become the fastest "notary office" in the mathematics community.

On November 21, the open-source formal verification community Lean and Mathlib issued a joint statement confirming the validity of Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. The two institutions jointly endorsed it, stating:

"We are fully confident that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct."

Verifying 17 million lines of code in 24 hours: How does Lean verify truth, and where are its boundaries?

Traditional mathematical breakthroughs rely on peer review of papers, judging the validity of each step of reasoning. But faced with over 250,000 pages of proof drafts that no one can fully understand in the short term, the formal verification software Lean has become the fastest "notary office" in the mathematics community.

Lean was founded in 2013 by Brazilian computer scientist Leonardo de Moura, initially developed at Microsoft Research, and later continued at Amazon Web Services (AWS). A rewritten version, Lean 4, was released in 2021 and is now supported by Lean FRO.

In this programming language and proof assistant, mathematicians must write each definition, prerequisite conclusion, and reasoning step into computer-readable code, which is then used by the program to verify the rigor of the logic. The community-shared mathematical library Mathlib, which began in 2017, has exceeded one million lines of code. Its documentation even includes a footnote about the Riemann Hypothesis, stating that constructing its proof is "worth a million dollars." Lean verified Peter Scholze's proof of condensed mathematics in 2021 and assisted Terence Tao in formalizing the proof of the Freiman-Ruzsa conjecture in polynomials in 2023. It is also the underlying tool used by Google DeepMind to build AlphaProof and has been used for code verification in Amazon Cedar policy language and Rust. However, the fact that the code can run and compile does not mean that the Riemann Hypothesis has been solved. In his Substack column, mathematician Kit Yates points out that while Lean verification is far more rigorous than having another AI judge it, experts still need to confirm three additional points: the code indeed proves the Riemann Hypothesis and not a weaker proposition; the definition faithfully reproduces standard objects such as the zeta function; and the reasoning does not include any additional assumptions. The Lean language reference manual also warns that the system cannot check whether new axioms are self-consistent, and one must be wary of placeholders that can "prove everything." The Lean community dared to make a decision in one day because Alpöge's codebase passed all four hard criteria proposed by Kevin Buzzard, a mathematician at Imperial College London, on November 12th. The first hurdle was verifying the "problem statement." This codebase directly depends on Mathlib, and the proven theorem points to the standard definition of the Riemann Hypothesis built into Mathlib—for all complex numbers whose zeta function is zero, except for trivial zeros such as -2, -4, and -6, the real part is 1/2. This definition has already been repeatedly verified by Lean and number theory experts. The second challenge is independent reproduction. This codebase, split into 14 compressed files and covering 175,187 modules, demands extremely high computational power; a single person needs approximately 100GB of memory and 70GB of hard drive space to complete the verification. MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland independently completed a flawless compilation using Lean and Mathlib v4.33.1, and the Mathlib files are consistent with the official cache. A joint statement shows that dozens of people have reproduced the compilation and generated completely identical original proof export files, totaling 61.6GB in size. The third challenge involves "behind-the-scenes manipulation." The community created a separate isolated file that only imports Mathlib and used two tools, `comparator` and `con-leche --compare`, to compare the results, both confirming that Alpöge's proved propositions completely matched the original Mathlib definitions. For axiom verification, Sutherland ran the `#print axioms` command on the five theorems in the main file `Main.lean`, showing that they depended only on three core axioms of Lean's seven standard axioms—`propext`, `Classical.choice`, and `Quot.sound`—and contained no `sorryAx`, all originating from the core library. "The probability of something fishy going on here is close to zero," Sutherland told Scientific American. The final hurdle was verifying the software itself. The official Lean kernel has a history of reliability vulnerabilities, which were patched within four hours of discovery. Mathematician Elliot Glazer estimated the probability of a vulnerability in Lean itself to be less than 1%. To isolate potential malicious code from the source code and avoid single kernel defects, the community skipped the source code and directly submitted the 61.6GB lazy export files to independent kernels in multiple languages ​​for cross-verification. Besides the official Lean kernel and `leanchecker` and `lean4lean`, which fully approved 175,187 modules, the Rust-based third-party kernel `nanoda` took 27 minutes and 42 seconds to accept a complete export; `con-leche` reviewed 1.468 million declarations in just 3 minutes and 15 seconds, rejecting none; `con-ron` also passed the test. The `con-leche` and `con-ron` statements themselves also come with a formal, self-consistent proof relative to set theory, mathematically ensuring that they cannot accept erroneous proofs. The validity of the verification is reflected in specific mathematical derivations. Combining existing formal results, the Sutherland page confirms that Robin's inequality and Lagarias' inequality regarding the sum of integer factors have been derived from this proof, also relying on only three standard axioms. In 1984, French mathematician Guy Robin proved that for any integer n greater than 5040, the sum of all its factors is less than 1.78. This intuitive proposition is completely equivalent to the Riemann Hypothesis—where γ is Euler's constant, and e^γ is approximately equal to 1.78. However, comparing the Lean Joint Statement with Sutherland's MIT verification page, this verification still has several technical boundaries that have not been fully resolved. While the Lean joint statement announced that both the `comparator` and the official kernel had passed, it did not disclose specific tool versions or detailed output logs. As of 12:55 UTC on November 21, Sutherland's end-to-end `comparator` run on Lean v4.36.0 had completed proposition comparison and axiom checking, but the kernel phase was still ongoing, and the default and strict kernels for Lean had not yet produced results; his previous builds and exports were not completed in the sandbox and are still awaiting comparison with the sandbox build results. As for the older versions `con-leche` and `con-ron` bundled with Lean v4.36.0, which returned exit code 2 because they did not support one type in the proof, Sutherland's page stated that this did not mean the proof was rejected. There are also discrepancies in the scope of the proofs. On November 20th, Elliot Glazer stated that the formalized proposition was actually a generalized Riemann Hypothesis, while Sutherland's page was more cautious: the master theorem is the Riemann Hypothesis as defined by Mathlib, and the other four theorems pertain to the Dirichlet L-function; the page only mentions "GRH" in this limited sense. Sutherland also cautioned that even if the axioms are checked and found to be correct, the final conclusion still relies on the premise that the Mathlib definition remains true to the mathematical intent and that the core itself is reliable. From Proof to "Judging" Looking behind the scenes, Claude's involvement was present at multiple stages, from proposing the proof to participating in the "judging." According to the research timeline provided by Alpöge, this work began with the "Stepanov determinant" on October 6th and was completed between late night on November 15th and early morning on November 16th, with only the three letters "GRH" remaining on the November 16th record. The timeline was reportedly compiled by Claude. Alpöge stated that he was responsible for pointing the way, and Claude subsequently proposed a breakthrough step—a chain of "theta lifts" approximately equal in length to the defined prime number and its square root, each lift corresponding to a "multiplicity" upon which classical function field proofs depend, but which is extremely difficult to find in the integer field. "Near the finish line, Claude far surpassed me. No, Claude was practically flying, dancing, and shining near the finish line," he wrote in a statement. Claude was still present during the verification phase. The signature at the beginning of the Sutherland verification page indicates that the entire check was run using Claude Code; and the con-leche that reviewed 1.468 million statements in 3 minutes and 15 seconds, according to Leonardo de Moura, the founder of Lean, in a blog post last month, is the first kernel written in Lean and proven to be self-consistent—both the code and the proof of self-consistency were completed by Claude, and rigorously reviewed by Joachim Breitner of Lean FRO. Because of the backing of formal self-consistent proofs, and because the final conclusions are consistent with multiple independent third-party kernels such as the Rust kernel nanoda, the verification of credibility does not depend on a single tool. This speed of progress exceeded Anthropic's own expectations three months prior. In August of this year, the company announced the results of its unpublished research using Claude in conjunction with Lean, which raised the lower bound of the zero-point ratio on the critical line from 41.6% to 67.2%, and passed the comparator test. At that time, Anthropic explicitly stated that it did not expect these techniques to ultimately prove the Riemann Hypothesis. Achieving this breakthrough just three months later, however, coincided with the sensitive window following the IPO on November 19th. Alpöge proactively admitted in a statement that "the precise timing was very bad," revealing that after completion, he asked Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei whether it could be made public, "and ultimately we figured out that there were indeed limitations to be followed." He denied negative speculation about the timing of the release, calling such "obvious cynical views" wrong, and admitted that he "couldn't wait any longer" and was willing to take full responsibility. The public frenzy and academic restraint: At 23:12 Beijing time on November 21, Lean's official announcement was released on the social media platform X, quickly sparking discussion in the tech community and mainstream academia. The AI ​​community was abuzz: AI researcher Yao Shunyu had already posted an exclamation on the evening of the 20th, "OMG, Riemann Hypothsis?!"; after the official statement was released, AI news writer Rohan Paul summarized it as "167 years later, the Riemann Hypothesis has finally been solved by AI," while the comment account Dr Singularity exclaimed, "What a time to be alive." Netizens also unearthed an old post from 2022 by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who jokingly asked on X when the Riemann Hypothesis would be solved, quipping, "Anthropic beat you to it." Mainstream scholars, however, were noticeably more cautious in their wording. On the morning of November 21, before Lean's official joint statement was released, Columbia University mathematics and physics professor Brian Greene posted that AI "may have solved the Riemann Hypothesis, which is above all other problems," but his wording was ambiguous, indicating it wasn't an independent verification by him. While Rutgers University's mathematics department chair Alex Kontorovich was increasingly optimistic about the successful proof, his only action on X that day was to retweet a report from *Quanta Magazine* about Alpöge's statement. Regarding the attribution of credit, the academic community also refuses to simplify this to "AI solving the problem alone." A mathematics and AI researcher at Princeton University emphasized that human involvement remains the best way to solve mathematical problems using large language models, and Alpöge should receive the same recognition as Claude. Sutherland, after independently compiling and passing the test, also called it a "victory for humanity." The more pressing reality is that while the machine has verified it, humans still cannot understand it. Thomas Bloom, a mathematician at the University of Manchester, stated on X that he couldn't distinguish whether what shocked him more was AI's claim to have proven the Riemann Hypothesis, or AI generating a logically coherent proof of over 250,000 pages in human-readable text. In his personal blog, Terence Tao, the 2006 Fields Medal winner, offered a preliminary assessment: the proof seems to integrate modern research findings from the Langlands program and arithmetic geometry, and verification and assimilation will still take time. "Fortunately," he noted, "this time, at least there's a human author to communicate with." Next, disassembling and simplifying this massive proof will become a core task for the mathematical community. Lean and the Mathlib community stated at the end of their announcement that they look forward to the mathematical community's subsequent work elucidating the new ideas in the proof. Alpöge himself also predicted that this astonishingly large proof "is likely to be significantly simplified, and may be achieved very soon." Even though the computer has given a positive response, the formal coronation of the Millennium Prize Problem still requires overcoming a long institutional hurdle. According to the rules of the Clay Mathematics Institute, the $1 million prize for the Millennium Prize Problem requires a formally published solution, at least two years of public scrutiny, and widespread international acceptance by the mathematical community. For Alpöge, what he calls "a dawn of something greater in the field of science" is still years away from truly settling down.
